effect_mechanism: WOCAT compilers attribute carbon gains to more vegetation: the Vallerani System in Burkina Faso raises biomass production many times over nearby unploughed soil, gabions and rock check dams in Somalia increase biomass and, through vegetation recovery and sediment accumulation, soil organic matter, a haffir in Somalia allows vegetation cover to regenerate, gradoni orchard terraces in Uzbekistan add below-ground organic matter through expanding roots, and the Magoye ripper in Zambia does so through less soil disturbance [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_1528_2012_biomass_above_ground_C, ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_7778_2026_biomass_above_ground_C, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_7778_2026_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_7777_2026_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_7553_2025_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C, ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_1139_2013_biomass_above_ground_C]. Emission ratings rest on tree nurseries enabled by sand dams in Kenya and tree cover building up over time at a masonry check dam in Ethiopia, and in the literature zai fields in Burkina Faso treated for several years had higher organic matter while trenches combined with vegetation raised soil organic carbon [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_1537_2012_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases, ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_6716_2023_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases, ev_soil_organic_carbon_kabo04_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_locat20_1]. A check-dam review cites check dams on China's Loess Plateau contributing to carbon sequestration, an effect that grows with time at both dam and watershed level as sediment accumulates [ev_carbon_sequestration_luca21_1]. A meta-analysis of Chinese soil and water conservation measures, available as a preprint, finds soil organic carbon 10.74% to 22.63% above the initial level after straw mulching across regions, and 3.36% and 75.77% higher after contour tillage in two regions within 5 to 10 years [ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_4]. The same preprint meta-analysis finds terracing raised soil organic carbon by 27%, 17.94% and 26.62% in three Chinese regions, with increases of 14.11% to 60.96% in regional subsets 11 to 30 years after construction [ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_5, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_6, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_7, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_8, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_9, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_10, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_11]. A Chinese meta-analysis, available as a preprint, reports fish-scale pits raising soil organic carbon storage by 79.86% on the Loess Plateau in years 11~30 [ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_12]. In Burkina Faso, soils on farms using soil and water conservation techniques had higher carbon and nitrogen contents than the control farm [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sawa11h1_3], and a review cites climate-smart packages of soil and water conservation structures with biological measures boosting soil carbon stock by three to seven times over business-as-usual [ev_soil_organic_carbon_tade23h1_3].
conditionality: Most units are compiler ratings from documented technology sheets in Niger, Uganda, Jordan, Tunisia, Sudan, Ethiopia, Rwanda, Haiti, Bangladesh, Bhutan and elsewhere, not measurements, many soil organic matter ratings carry no comment, and soil organic matter and emission ratings are proxies rather than measured sequestration; the Bangladesh emission rationale (crops absorbing more carbon dioxide under higher cropping intensity) is not long-term storage, and the Bhutan sheet describes organic matter moving downslope within each terrace [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_4284_2018_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_6891_2023_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C]. The literature is mixed: trenches in Mexico lowered soil nitrogen and carbon, and a zai trial in Burkina Faso found no significant change in organic matter by the end of the experiment even though biomass rose [ev_soil_organic_carbon_locat20_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_roose93_1]. The Loess Plateau check-dam finding is a secondary citation in a review, with no magnitude in the quoted passage [ev_carbon_sequestration_luca21_1]. The Chinese figures come from a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, in an upper-middle-income country. Several are the values for the duration window with the greatest increase rather than a pooled estimate, and the duration subsets overlap the regional ones [ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_8, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_12]. The Burkina Faso result is a carbon content on farm soils, not a stock change, and the three-to-sevenfold stock gain is a review's citation of a package that includes biological measures, very large for structures and to be read with caution [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sawa11h1_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_tade23h1_3]. Paired soil samples from Zambian fields under planting basins or ripping (bundled with reduced tillage), with crop residues hardly retained, showed no significant difference in organic carbon from conventional fields [ev_soil_organic_carbon_umar11_4].

justification.mechanism: WOCAT compilers attribute carbon gains to more vegetation: the Vallerani System in Burkina Faso raises biomass production many times over nearby unploughed soil, gabions and rock check dams in Somalia increase biomass and, through vegetation recovery and sediment accumulation, soil organic matter, a haffir in Somalia allows vegetation cover to regenerate, gradoni orchard terraces in Uzbekistan add below-ground organic matter through expanding roots, and the Magoye ripper in Zambia does so through less soil disturbance [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_1528_2012_biomass_above_ground_C, ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_7778_2026_biomass_above_ground_C, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_7778_2026_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_7777_2026_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_7553_2025_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C, ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_1139_2013_biomass_above_ground_C]. Emission ratings rest on tree nurseries enabled by sand dams in Kenya and tree cover building up over time at a masonry check dam in Ethiopia, and in the literature zai fields in Burkina Faso treated for several years had higher organic matter while trenches combined with vegetation raised soil organic carbon [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_1537_2012_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases, ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_6716_2023_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases, ev_soil_organic_carbon_kabo04_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_locat20_1]. A check-dam review cites check dams on China's Loess Plateau contributing to carbon sequestration, an effect that grows with time at both dam and watershed level as sediment accumulates [ev_carbon_sequestration_luca21_1]. A meta-analysis of Chinese soil and water conservation measures, available as a preprint, finds soil organic carbon 10.74% to 22.63% above the initial level after straw mulching across regions, and 3.36% and 75.77% higher after contour tillage in two regions within 5 to 10 years [ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_4]. The same preprint meta-analysis finds terracing raised soil organic carbon by 27%, 17.94% and 26.62% in three Chinese regions, with increases of 14.11% to 60.96% in regional subsets 11 to 30 years after construction [ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_5, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_6, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_7, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_8, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_9, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_10, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_11]. A Chinese meta-analysis, available as a preprint, reports fish-scale pits raising soil organic carbon storage by 79.86% on the Loess Plateau in years 11~30 [ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_12]. In Burkina Faso, soils on farms using soil and water conservation techniques had higher carbon and nitrogen contents than the control farm [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sawa11h1_3], and a review cites climate-smart packages of soil and water conservation structures with biological measures boosting soil carbon stock by three to seven times over business-as-usual [ev_soil_organic_carbon_tade23h1_3].
justification.conditionality: Most units are compiler ratings from documented technology sheets in Niger, Uganda, Jordan, Tunisia, Sudan, Ethiopia, Rwanda, Haiti, Bangladesh, Bhutan and elsewhere, not measurements, many soil organic matter ratings carry no comment, and soil organic matter and emission ratings are proxies rather than measured sequestration; the Bangladesh emission rationale (crops absorbing more carbon dioxide under higher cropping intensity) is not long-term storage, and the Bhutan sheet describes organic matter moving downslope within each terrace [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_4284_2018_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases, ev_soil_organic_carbon_wocat_6891_2023_soil_organic_matter_below_ground_C]. The literature is mixed: trenches in Mexico lowered soil nitrogen and carbon, and a zai trial in Burkina Faso found no significant change in organic matter by the end of the experiment even though biomass rose [ev_soil_organic_carbon_locat20_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_roose93_1]. The Loess Plateau check-dam finding is a secondary citation in a review, with no magnitude in the quoted passage [ev_carbon_sequestration_luca21_1]. The Chinese figures come from a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, in an upper-middle-income country. Several are the values for the duration window with the greatest increase rather than a pooled estimate, and the duration subsets overlap the regional ones [ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_8, ev_soil_organic_carbon_zhang26h2_12]. The Burkina Faso result is a carbon content on farm soils, not a stock change, and the three-to-sevenfold stock gain is a review's citation of a package that includes biological measures, very large for structures and to be read with caution [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sawa11h1_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_tade23h1_3]. Paired soil samples from Zambian fields under planting basins or ripping (bundled with reduced tillage), with crop residues hardly retained, showed no significant difference in organic carbon from conventional fields [ev_soil_organic_carbon_umar11_4].

effect_mechanism: Groundwater recharge now counts as a component of catchment water yield, so this row holds two kinds of evidence. Most units report recharge and rising water tables at or near capture structures: the proportion of runoff infiltrated through check dams can reach more than 50%, with recharge linked to episodic storm events [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_luca21_1]; groundwater tables rise in the vicinity of filled check dams, and sand dams can raise the local groundwater [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_fran21_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ritc21_1]; in India additional recharge from check dams and other water harvesting structures was estimated at 480 million cubic meters per annum, groundwater levels rose in 16 of 21 non-desert districts with an average increase of 1.42 meters, and a state survey found levels increased in 22 of the 31 districts [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_verm19_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_verm19_3, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_verm19_2]; the Uttarakhand water budget shows aquifer recharge up 3.3 percent and water yield from catchment areas up 4.9 percent [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_utk22_5], and ISRO survey data record increased recharge in treated areas [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_iegind11_3]; terraces would cause a groundwater recharge of 15 to 25% of rainfall, and modelling of contour ridges in Morocco estimates a 50% increase in recharge [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_roose06_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_willem21_1]; stone bunds, zaï and half-moons applied at watershed scale increase ground water level, and in Burkina Faso improved well levels are linked to SWC measures that control surface runoff and improve infiltration [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_zoug14_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_kabo04_1]; communities in Mauritania, spate beneficiaries in Yemen and an Ethiopian public-works assessment report rising well levels, increased groundwater or water-table improvements [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mrt14_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_yem12_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_yem12_2, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_eth16_7]; and a review lists aquifer recharge among benefits cited for water harvesting [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_saru19_1]. The two reductions are measured on flow leaving the treated land: On China's Loess Plateau, a large campaign of check-dam construction carried out since the 1970s to retain floodwater and intercept soil sediments reduced streamflow by approximately 39% [ev_water_yield_luca21_1], and in the Maghreb mechanised bund systems, built with large machines that scrape a 4 to 10 m strip to raise bunds 1.5 to 2 m high every 30 to 50 m, considerably reduce the water collected in downstream hill reservoirs and cost 10 to 25% of the cultivable area [ev_water_yield_roos10_1]. In Burkina Faso, cited studies show soil and water conservation techniques improving the availability of ground water in many villages, especially large rock bunds known as digues filtrantes [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_sawa11h1_6]. Embrapa says its barraginhas in Brazil help recharge groundwater by raising the water table and revitalise springs and rivers [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mira19_6].
conditionality: This row is for downstream users and basin planners: it asks what capturing water upstream does to the water that reaches streams and reservoirs below, not whether the farm that captures it has more. The two sides are measured in different places: the gains are groundwater and well levels at or near the structures, the losses are streamflow and reservoir inflow below large-scale works — a check-dam campaign built to retain floodwater and mechanised bunds. The class follows the sub-practice vote. The terracing row holds the strongest result, moderate positive, on the terrace recharge estimate and the Moroccan contour-ridge modelling [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_roose06_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_willem21_1]. The runoff-catchment row (check dams, sand dams, small reservoirs) holds slight positive, because it carries the Loess Plateau streamflow reduction alongside its recharge reports [ev_water_yield_luca21_1], and the spate and cross-family rows also hold slight positive. The in-field row leans slightly negative: it holds the Maghreb mechanised-bund reduction and the Peruvian trench baseflow finding against the Mauritanian well levels and the Andean recharge that cannot be generalised [ev_water_yield_roos10_1, ev_water_regulation_locat20_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mrt14_1, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_locat20_1]. The weighted median of the positive rows is slight positive, below the pooled moderate. No unit compares downstream flow with and without the works, so the slight positive class says that capture recharges local aquifers, not that more water reaches users downstream. The recharge side has limits in its own sources: the sand-dam effect is often limited in space and time [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ritc21_1]; in India, pumping from tube wells that land-owning farmers sank as the water table rose has possibly wiped out any increases in recharge from the watershed treatments, and without data from untreated sites the project impact is unclear [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_iegind11_4, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_iegind11_3]; in Burkina Faso the number of wells with water year round has not increased significantly since SWC began [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_kabo04_2]; and catchment-level recharge gains in the Andes are plausible but cannot be generalised [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_locat20_1]. Most recharge units are secondary citations, programme reports or modelling, and few state a size, which caps the class. On the loss side, the 39% is a figure the check-dam review cites from another study (Shi et al., 2015) for one Chinese region [ev_water_yield_luca21_1], and the Maghreb reduction is a narrative from a Moroccan expert manual with no figure for the water lost downstream; the 10 to 25% is cultivable area, not water [ev_water_yield_roos10_1]. Against both, the downstream streamflow impacts of small-scale water storage systems have in other cases been limited, even when implemented widely [ev_water_yield_rock10_1], and trenches in the Peruvian Andes had little effect on increasing baseflow, with hydrogeological characteristics key to explaining their impact [ev_water_regulation_locat20_1]. The digues filtrantes finding is cited from another study, with no figures [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_sawa11h1_6]. The barraginha recharge statement is Embrapa's self-assessment of its own technology, with no measurement behind it [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_mira19_6].

conditionality: Recharge stands in for catchment yield; no unit measures flow leaving the catchment. The Cameroonian source flags that the drainage could reach the unterraced piedmonts, a much more fragile environment [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_roose06_1]. conditionality: WOCAT figures are the compiler's own cost tables for the documented technology, summed and converted to USD with the sheet's own exchange rate; they are not market prices, and older sheets treat every costed item as per hectare, so converted figures range from under a dollar to tens of thousands of USD per hectare; the sub-dollar sheets for Uganda and Niger and the Yemen sheet's figure look like entry or conversion problems rather than real costs. effect_mechanism: In low- and lower-middle-income settings the pooled per-hectare costs are up-front establishment and treatment costs. An independent evaluation of two World Bank-supported India watershed projects reports treatment unit costs of US$261 per hectare in the Integrated Watershed Development Project and US$217/ha in the Karnataka project [ev_project_cost_iegind11_10, ev_project_cost_iegind11_11]. A Yemen completion report gives average investment costs for spate systems of USD 800- 1200/ha, of which the farmer's 15-20% share comes to US$ 150-200/ha [ev_project_cost_yem12_8]. Two WOCAT technology sheets add compiler-reported establishment costs: 2000.00 USD per hectare for orchard terraces in Uzbekistan, a total spread over 1.6 ha [ev_project_cost_wocat_7553_2025_establishment], and 147.30 USD per hectare for gabion and rock check-dam gully control in Somalia, a total spread over 160 ha [ev_project_cost_wocat_7778_2026_establishment].
conditionality: The figures measure different things: watershed treatment cost per hectare treated in India, spate-system investment in Yemen, and WOCAT compilers' own cost tables converted with each sheet's exchange rate, which are not market prices; none is a cost per hectare of degraded land restored, and no price-year adjustment is made across them. The India evaluator calls the US$261 per hectare cost high by Indian standards, and the US$217/ha cost below the central government norm [ev_project_cost_iegind11_10, ev_project_cost_iegind11_11]; the Yemen report calls the farmer contribution comparatively high [ev_project_cost_yem12_8]. The Somali figure spreads a whole gully-control package over the treated area, which keeps it low per hectare, while the Uzbek terrace figure is a small orchard plot, so the spread from 147.30 to 2000.00 USD per hectare reflects practice and denominator as much as cost. All four countries are in the low- or lower-middle-income target band.

effect_mechanism: Water harvesting buffers dry periods by storing or infiltrating water, but only the storage practices show a large effect: zai pits reduce the impact of dry spells of a few weeks when soil water storage is sufficient, runoff ponds in semi-arid Brazil supply supplemental irrigation and production cisterns supply livestock water, cisterns in China are reported to mitigate frequent droughts, and public-works interventions in Ethiopia raised water availability. WOCAT compilers for Vallerani micro-catchments, ponds, check dams, terraces, stone lines and water-spreading weirs judge drought impacts reduced through stored water, infiltration and soil moisture retention, and households in a Rwandan land husbandry and water harvesting project proved more resilient than controls to the 2016 drought. In a Kenyan catchment with sand dams the number of people exposed to droughts fell from 420 to 0 while a control catchment stayed at 600 [ev_drought_hazard_lasage08_1]. A Burkina Faso review concludes that soil and water conservation techniques helped reduce vulnerability to drought and famine [ev_drought_hazard_sawa11h1_7]. In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, the plots without mulch were the ones particularly affected by the dry spells of the season [ev_drought_hazard_sime15h2_1]. In Brazil, Embrapa describes its barraginhas, small semicircular runoff-retention basins dug along runoff paths in pastures and croplands, as storing water in the soil by infiltration and easing the effects of droughts on crops in the lowlands [ev_drought_hazard_mira19_8].
conditionality: The class follows the sub-practice vote, not the pooled result. Only the storage family (sand dams, ponds, cisterns, check dams) holds a strong result, and that rests largely on the Kenyan sand-dam catchment table [ev_drought_hazard_lasage08_1]. The in-field row (zaï, mulch), the terracing row (the Rwandan programme and terrace sheets), the spate row (marab floodplain farming in Jordan, water-spreading weirs in Ethiopia) and the cross-family row (Ethiopian public works, Brazilian production cisterns, the Tunisian programme, the Burkina Faso review) each hold slight positive, so the roll-up is slight positive rather than the pooled strong [ev_drought_hazard_roose93_1, ev_drought_hazard_rwa18_6, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_5770_2020_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_6715_2023_drought_impacts, ev_drought_hazard_arega24_4, ev_drought_hazard_castro22_2, ev_drought_hazard_iegtun13_1, ev_drought_hazard_sawa11h1_7]. Much of the pool is practitioner judgement from technology sheets or expert assertion (Brazilian research and programme authors, a lender evaluation in China without measurement), and only the Rwanda unit, reported second-hand in a completion report, and the Kenyan sand-dam catchment table, whose values are likely interview-derived, rest on comparisons against controls [ev_drought_hazard_lasage08_1]. The Ethiopian study notes vegetation greenness still tracked local drought severity, the Haiti compiler states the impact is not yet measured, and the zai effect depends on soil storage capacity. Storage itself runs short in prolonged drought: subsurface dams in Brazil tended to dry out in a rainless year, and consecutive drought years in Tunisia limited soil-conservation benefits; these units record no benefit at that point, a shortfall rather than damage [ev_drought_hazard_cirilo03_2, ev_drought_hazard_iegtun13_1]. That Burkina Faso conclusion is the author's overall judgement, with no measured drought-year contrast behind it [ev_drought_hazard_sawa11h1_7]. The Ethiopian dry-spell finding is a field observation of which plots wilted, not a tested yield contrast [ev_drought_hazard_sime15h2_1]. The barraginha statement is Embrapa's self-assessment of its own technology, with no measured drought contrast and no normal-year reference [ev_drought_hazard_mira19_8].

effect_mechanism: Terraces, contour stone bunds and lines, check dams, sand dams and water-spreading structures slow and spread runoff and retain water and sediment, lowering peak discharges and lengthening flood rise times; in a semi-arid Tunisian catchment a combined treatment cut the runoff volume of 71 single-peak floods by 50%, and WOCAT compilers for many of these structures judge downstream flooding reduced. Users of small reservoirs in Ghana perceive fewer rainy-season floods, and spate and diversion structures in Yemen are said to control floods. A check-dam review cites check dams mitigating flooding and significantly reducing peak flow in Iran and check-dam sequences proving effective against strong floods in Italian torrents, and small hill dams in Morocco are credited with damping damage in the serious 2002-2003 floods [ev_flood_hazard_luca21_1, ev_flood_hazard_luca21_2, ev_flood_hazard_roos10_1]. Embrapa credits its barraginhas, small runoff-retention basins dug along runoff paths in Brazil, with easing floods as well [ev_flood_hazard_mira19_7].
conditionality: Most units are practitioner judgements from technology sheets, and catchment-scale measurement is scarce, with a review calling the terrace effect on peak flow uncertain; the Tunisian result bundles rangeland closure and gully stone-filling with the bunds, and the Yemen and Uttarakhand statements are lender self-reported. Direction depends on design: diversion banquettes in Niger and runoff-diversion dikes raised peak flows, larger sand dams increase flooding risk, a conservation-tillage sheet from the Philippines rated flood impacts worse, and a farm pond in India was rated neutral. The same review finds check dams have a minimal effect against extreme floods, especially where ill-designed or poorly maintained; its positive cases are secondary citations, and the Italian ones are mountain torrent control in a high-income setting [ev_flood_hazard_luca21_3, ev_flood_hazard_luca21_1, ev_flood_hazard_luca21_2]. The barraginha flood statement is Embrapa's self-assessment of its own technology, unmeasured, and a landscape-scale effect rather than one on the adopting farm [ev_flood_hazard_mira19_7].

justification.mechanism: Terraces, contour stone bunds and lines, check dams, sand dams and water-spreading structures slow and spread runoff and retain water and sediment, lowering peak discharges and lengthening flood rise times; in a semi-arid Tunisian catchment a combined treatment cut the runoff volume of 71 single-peak floods by 50%, and WOCAT compilers for many of these structures judge downstream flooding reduced. Users of small reservoirs in Ghana perceive fewer rainy-season floods, and spate and diversion structures in Yemen are said to control floods. A check-dam review cites check dams mitigating flooding and significantly reducing peak flow in Iran and check-dam sequences proving effective against strong floods in Italian torrents, and small hill dams in Morocco are credited with damping damage in the serious 2002-2003 floods [ev_flood_hazard_luca21_1, ev_flood_hazard_luca21_2, ev_flood_hazard_roos10_1]. Embrapa credits its barraginhas, small runoff-retention basins dug along runoff paths in Brazil, with easing floods as well [ev_flood_hazard_mira19_7].
justification.conditionality: Most units are practitioner judgements from technology sheets, and catchment-scale measurement is scarce, with a review calling the terrace effect on peak flow uncertain; the Tunisian result bundles rangeland closure and gully stone-filling with the bunds, and the Yemen and Uttarakhand statements are lender self-reported. Direction depends on design: diversion banquettes in Niger and runoff-diversion dikes raised peak flows, larger sand dams increase flooding risk, a conservation-tillage sheet from the Philippines rated flood impacts worse, and a farm pond in India was rated neutral. The same review finds check dams have a minimal effect against extreme floods, especially where ill-designed or poorly maintained; its positive cases are secondary citations, and the Italian ones are mountain torrent control in a high-income setting [ev_flood_hazard_luca21_3, ev_flood_hazard_luca21_1, ev_flood_hazard_luca21_2]. The barraginha flood statement is Embrapa's self-assessment of its own technology, unmeasured, and a landscape-scale effect rather than one on the adopting farm [ev_flood_hazard_mira19_7].

effect_mechanism: WOCAT compilers for planting pits and stone lines, zai/tassa pits and contour bunds in Niger and conservation tillage in Kenya and Zambia judge downstream flooding reduced; the sheets describe no mechanism, and the Zambia compiler adds that the effect holds only if the practice is applied on a large scale.
conditionality: All units are practitioner judgements, not measurements, mostly rated slight; the conservation-tillage sheet from the Philippines rated flood impacts worse, and conservation-tillage sheets are a loose fit for an in-situ water-harvesting family.

effect_mechanism: Water harvesting and conservation structures capture runoff and raise soil moisture so rainfed crops yield more, especially in dry years and low-rainfall areas; stored water allows supplemental irrigation and extra crops, and sediment and organic matter trapped behind structures add fertility. Meta-analyses now carry much of the evidence: A meta-analysis of traditional in-situ water harvesting finds a pooled yield gain of 71% over controls, with 142% for infiltration pits, 91% for mulching, 69% for soil and stone bunds, 48% for terraces and 74% for tied ridging [ev_crop_yield_tefe24_1, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_2, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_3, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_4, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_5, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_6]; a synthesis of Ethiopian studies gives mean grain-yield differences of 322 kg per hectare for stone bunds, 554.3 for tied ridges and 629.2 for mulching [ev_crop_yield_adim16_1, ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_4]; a sub-Saharan conservation agriculture meta-analysis finds yields 3.7% above conventional tillage overall, 8.4% for maize when all three principles are applied and 12.5% at sites with under 400 mm of seasonal rainfall, with the gain growing slowly over time [ev_crop_yield_corb20_1, ev_crop_yield_corb20_4, ev_crop_yield_corb20_6, ev_crop_yield_corb20_10]; and a terracing meta-analysis finds biomass on terraces about 1.94 times that on slopes, and reviewed studies report terraced teff, barley and maize yields at least two times those on slopes and 20% gains on young bench terraces in Peru [ev_crop_yield_wei16_1, ev_crop_yield_wei16_2, ev_crop_yield_wei16_4]. In Burkina Faso stone bunds raised sorghum yields by 33% to 55% and by about 142% with compost, on-farm trials in Mozambique gave maize gains of 504 to 800 kg per hectare on planting basins and direct-seeded plots, in Malawi's El Niño season ground cover raised maize from 247 to 432 kg per hectare, and silt farmland behind check dams on China's Loess Plateau yields 6–10 times more than sloping farmland [ev_crop_yield_zoug14_2, ev_crop_yield_zoug14_4, ev_crop_yield_thierf15_3, ev_crop_yield_boil19_2, ev_crop_yield_luca21_1]. Stored water stabilises output: Indian farmers reported crop-failure chances falling from 20% to 6% in the rainy season and from 100% to 5–10% in winter with a farm pond, sand dams cut crop failure against a control catchment in Kenya, and WOCAT compilers across many technology sheets judge crop, fodder and animal production increased [ev_yield_stability_pals23_1, ev_yield_stability_pals23_2, ev_crop_yield_lasage08_1]. In a Zimbabwe enterprise budget first-year planting-basin conservation farming yielded 1520 kg of maize per hectare against 400 kg on the fertilised conventional arm [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_2]. Newer field trials point the same way: In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, maize stalk mulch raised maize yield over no mulch at both sites in both seasons, and planting basins did so in 2012 [ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_1, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_2, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_3, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_4, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_6, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_8]. In Rwanda, vetiver mulch raised maize to 8089 kg per hectare against 4755 on flat rainfed plots [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_1], and in the same trial runoff from the terrace waterways, collected in a dug, lined pond and applied by a gravity drip kit as supplementary irrigation, gave 11982 kg per hectare [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_3]. In Burkina Faso, crop yields in years of average rainfall rose by 63–74 per cent on farms using rock bunds and by over 100 per cent on farms using zaï [ev_crop_yield_sawa11h1_1, ev_crop_yield_sawa11h1_2]. On crusted degraded soil in Burkina Faso, 30-cm zaï and 1-m half-moons with compost gave 408 and 1372 kg of millet per hectare where direct seeding gave none [ev_crop_yield_zour25h1_1, ev_crop_yield_zour25h1_2]. In Zimbabwe's El Niño drought season, maize under no-till with a residue mulch yielded 31.8% more than under conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_mash25h1_1]. A review cites soil and water conservation structures combined with biological measures raising wheat production by 30–45% over business-as-usual [ev_crop_yield_tade23h1_2]. Soils on Burkina Faso farms using soil and water conservation techniques had higher nitrogen contents than the control farm, used here as a component [ev_soil_nitrogen_sawa11h1_4]. Primary trials and surveys from eastern and southern Africa now stand in for second-hand Zambia readings. In on-farm trials in Ethiopia, ripper plus tied ridging with fertiliser gave 1775 kg of maize per hectare against 1458 under conventional maresha ploughing with the same fertiliser, and 1076 against 945 kg of tef [ev_crop_yield_rock09_1, ev_crop_yield_rock09_4]; in Tanzania, ripping and pitting combined with fertilisation gave yields 1.5–2.2 times those of conventional ploughing with the same fertilisation [ev_crop_yield_rock09_11]; and at Chipata, Zambia, basins with fertiliser gave 6660 kg of maize per hectare against 3153 under conventional practice [ev_crop_yield_rock09_13]. In Zambia's 2001/2 season hand-hoe conservation-farming basins gave 3,054 kg of maize per hectare against 1,339 under ploughing, and a regression controlling for planting date, hybrid seed and fertiliser puts the gain from the basins themselves closer to 700 kg per hectare for maize and 400 to 500 kg for cotton [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_2, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_3]; a later survey of Zambian conservation-agriculture households reports 5.2 t of maize per hectare in basins against 1.8 under the hand hoe [ev_crop_yield_umar11_1]. A meta-analysis of tied-ridge-furrow experiments finds tied ridges without fertiliser or mulch yielded 17% more sorghum grain than flat planting [ev_crop_yield_makm21_1]. In Madagascar, rice sown without tillage on a dead mulch and rotated averaged 2.8 against 2.6 t per hectare on lowland and 2.4 against 2.1 on hillside fields, and year-to-year variability fell after consecutive years under the system (a 6% and a 13% decrease in the coefficient of variation) [ev_crop_yield_brue14_1, ev_crop_yield_brue14_2, ev_yield_stability_brue14_3, ev_yield_stability_brue14_4]. Crop-model (APSIM) runs on semi-arid Zimbabwe weather give higher maize yields under conservation agriculture than under ploughing when aggregated across seasons, and more stable yields across different types of seasons [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_5, ev_yield_stability_faocr11_6]. In a Zimbabwe household panel, conservation agriculture (mostly planting basins, with residue mulch and rotation on some plots) improved maize yields both when rainfall was above average and during times of drought, and sorghum and cowpea yields during drought [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3, ev_crop_yield_mich19_4, ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. A review of conservation agriculture in Zambia also cites planting basins plus lime raising yields by 68% [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_1], a simulated gain of around 40% for the whole conservation farming package [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_6], higher soil moisture improving yields in poor seasons [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_3], and global syntheses: reduced tillage and crop residue management associated with a 106% increase in cereal yields, an average yield improvement of over 100% for smallholder conservation agriculture across 286 developing-country case studies, and a slight increase over conventional tillage, growing over time and especially in dry conditions, across 25 long-term trials [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_13, ev_crop_yield_arsl15_15, ev_crop_yield_arsl15_16]. Grain per unit of rain rises with capture in a set of East and Southern African trials: the best conservation-farming practice per site gave yield increases ranging from 20 to 120% over conventional tillage whilst rain water productivity improved with 10–50% [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. In an on-farm trial at Houndé, Burkina Faso, stone rows with zaï pits, every arm also receiving manure, raised maize grain to 4457 kg per hectare with NPK and urea against 2157 kg under the farmers' practice of oxen ploughing with NPK and urea, and to 3768 kg averaged over the fertility options, and lifted rain water productivity from 3.10 to 6.61 kg per hectare per mm [ev_crop_yield_koro17_1, ev_crop_yield_koro17_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_1]. A review reports that contour tied-ridging in eastern Sudan gave the highest water use efficiency of the treatments compared [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. The water-productivity evidence points the same way: FAO compilers list improved water use efficiency among the main benefits of rainwater harvesting, the WOCAT guideline authors find that all water harvesting groups indicate improved water use efficiency, mostly high to medium, through reduced evaporation loss and better soil water availability, and a review sentence, citing earlier work, says capture approaches often lead also to higher water productivity because denser canopies shade the soil [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock10_1]. The FAO compilers rate improving water productivity at the top of their scale for the conservation agriculture group [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_2]. They rate improving water productivity for the cross-slope barrier group at the middle mark of their scale [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_3]. For the WOCAT water harvesting groups the guideline authors' marks for improving water productivity run from the lowest positive mark for floodwater and microcatchment harvesting to the middle mark for macrocatchment harvesting [ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_3].
conditionality: Held out of the class, as a caveat on where the practice performs rather than as production evidence: where rainfall is heavy the practice can lower yields through waterlogging, and the authors say so. Annual rainfall above 1000 mm affected the performance of Ethiopian soil and water conservation practices negatively, which the synthesis puts down to water logging on the furrows of structures, and fanya juu and soil bunds were associated with yield losses of 54 to 193 kg per hectare [ev_crop_yield_adim16_6, ev_crop_yield_adim16_2]; plots with bunds yielded less than non-conserved plots in high-rainfall western Amhara [ev_crop_yield_schmidt12_10]; in the Sudanian zone of Cameroon, where rain exceeds 80 mm a day and 1,200 mm a year, sorghum in zaï pits yielded less than flat-cultivated fields because of frequent waterlogging and the risk of nutrient leaching [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]; 92% of the data in a conservation agriculture review show mulch cover in high-rainfall areas lowering yields through waterlogging [ev_crop_yield_rusin11_3]; and at sites with over 1,200 mm of seasonal rainfall conservation agriculture yielded 4.3% less than conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_corb20_7]. In a wetter sub-humid Kenyan site, ridged plots with fertiliser gave the lowest yields, slightly below conventional practice, which the authors say can probably be explained by waterlogging caused by ridging [ev_crop_yield_rock09_6]. Read these as a siting limit: the practice should not be applied where rainfall is that heavy. Other measured losses do count against the class: bunds cut yields by up to 7% in the first few years in Ethiopia, and stone bunds in semi-arid Tanzania reduced maize yield by 13% [ev_crop_yield_adim16_7, ev_crop_yield_adim16_9]. The sub-Saharan conservation agriculture meta-analysis finds no significant gain for crops other than maize, and outperformance of conventional tillage only with no-tillage systems rather than planting basins or minimum tillage [ev_crop_yield_corb20_3, ev_crop_yield_corb20_9]; a maize meta-regression finds conservation agriculture consistently underperforms on high-clay soils in very wet seasons, though at median rainfall and clay it outperforms conventional practice even without fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_stew18_3, ev_crop_yield_stew18_4]; and in drought seasons in Mozambique and Zimbabwe conservation agriculture gave no harvest or yielded less than conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_thierf15_1, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_7]. In Algeria farmers lost 5 to 15% of their cropped area to banquettes without seeing yields improve, legume yields between banquettes showed no significant gain, and a Moroccan farmer saw no yield improvement between banquettes imposed by technicians [ev_crop_yield_arab04_1, ev_crop_yield_arab04_2, ev_crop_yield_roos10_2]. Other nulls and negatives: conservation promoted mostly off-farm had no yield effect, benefits in Ethiopia appeared only once structures were maintained for at least seven years, diversion banquettes in Niger cut yields, and soil salinisation can appear on check-dam farmland [ev_crop_yield_luca21_1]. Outside the meta-analyses the pool mixes independent evaluations with lender completion-report figures, bundled watershed programmes, reviews quoting ranges from earlier studies, a farmer survey reported in a preprint and many practitioner judgements; much of the zai and planting-basin gain rides on added manure, compost or fertiliser [ev_yield_stability_pals23_1, ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1]. In the Malawi El Nino survey banking, the reinforcement of ridges while the crop is growing, cut maize from 245 to 153 kg per hectare, so some in-field practices lowered yield in that season [ev_crop_yield_boil19_5]. Planting basins gave no significant gain over no mulch in 2011 at either Ethiopian site (4239 against 4171 and 4265 against 4131 kg per hectare) [ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_5, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_7]. Rwandan contour ridges were not significantly different from flat rainfed plots (5937 against 4755 kg per hectare) [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_2]. The Burkina Faso zaï and half-moon contrasts are against land where direct seeding produced no grain, with compost added to the pits, so they measure bringing degraded land into production rather than an improvement on a cropped field. The Burkina Faso farm gains are for years the authors call average rainfall, with compost on the bunded fields. The Zimbabwe residue-mulch gain is one on-station season with no normal-year comparison, and the mulch is bundled with no-till [ev_crop_yield_mash25h1_1]. The wheat figure is a review's citation of a package that includes biological measures [ev_crop_yield_tade23h1_2]. The Rwandan pond result is a bundle — terrace runoff capture, a lined storage pond and drip irrigation — so the yield is delivered through irrigation hardware and cannot be read as a pure capture effect; it is one season of a randomised trial in which every plot received farmyard manure and mineral fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_3]. The East African and Zambian trial gains are bundles. In Ethiopia the comparator carried the same fertiliser, but without fertiliser neither improved tillage nor fertiliser alone raised maize significantly, and the 20–50% tef gain without fertiliser was not significant [ev_crop_yield_rock09_2, ev_crop_yield_rock09_3]; the Tanzanian ripping-or-pitting arms are bundled with reduced tillage [ev_crop_yield_rock09_11]; and the Chipata basins carried improved seed against a conventional practice with extremely low fertiliser, in seasons of well-above-average rainfall, a gain the authors say cannot be fully explained [ev_crop_yield_rock09_13]. Some trial arms lost: pitting with fertiliser was the lowest-yielding treatment at Machakos, at 1.2 against 1.6 t per hectare under conventional practice [ev_crop_yield_rock09_9], and at the more arid Kenyan sites each site recorded complete crop failures in two out of three and four seasons, which the treatments did not avert; water harvesting is not irrigation [ev_crop_yield_rock09_10]. The Zambian 2001/2 raw contrast is one season with no normal-year reference and mixes the basin effect with higher input use, since most basin farmers received hybrid seed, fertiliser and lime on credit; the regression figure is the cleaner estimate, and even its basin dummy also picks up extra weeding labour and lime [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_2]. The later Zambian survey yields are farmer self-reports with large spreads, and the basin gain over ploughing (5.2 against 3.8 t per hectare) was not significant [ev_crop_yield_umar11_1, ev_crop_yield_umar11_2]; a national Zambian smallholder panel finds no significant maize yield effect of planting basins under any of its estimators [ev_crop_yield_burk12_1]; and paired soil samples on Zambian fields under basins or ripping (bundled with reduced tillage), with residues hardly retained, showed no significant difference in nitrogen [ev_soil_nitrogen_umar11_6]. The Zimbabwe panel keeps drought-season and normal-season results apart: in average rainfall periods conservation agriculture had no significant impact on any crop, in another specification it decreased maize yields by itself, and it did not mitigate rainfall-shortfall or surplus losses for millet and groundnut, so its gains appear only in seasons away from the average [ev_crop_yield_mich19_1, ev_crop_yield_mich19_2, ev_crop_yield_mich19_6, ev_crop_yield_mich19_7]. The tied-ridge meta-analysis finds no significant millet gain over flat planting and no significant difference when grass mulch was added to the ridges, and its sorghum observation count is internally inconsistent [ev_crop_yield_makm21_3, ev_crop_yield_makm21_2, ev_crop_yield_makm21_1]. In Madagascar the severe drought of 2007–2008 could not be offset by the system, and the pooled comparison showed no change in yield variance, the stability gain appearing only after consecutive years; the rice gains bundle no-till, mulch and rotation [ev_crop_yield_brue14_5, ev_yield_stability_brue14_7]. The crop-model results are simulations that bundle residue cover, better infiltration and fertiliser targeting; under sub-humid weather the model gives no difference [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_4], and in seasons with 230 mm and 176 mm of in-crop rainfall there was total crop failure under both systems [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_2]. Farmer reports of basin yields of >1 tonnes per hectare in poor-rainfall seasons, against total failure under ploughing, compare fertilised basins with unfertilised ploughing, which the author calls too confounded [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_9]. The remaining Zambia and global figures are cited secondhand in Arslan and colleagues' literature review, and none has a normal-year comparison: the 68% gain is for planting basins plus lime application, with timely conventional farming giving 50% in the same trials [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_1]; the roughly 40% gain is a simulation of the whole conservation farming package, through early planting and improved soil quality [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_6]; the 106% is for reduced tillage together with residue management [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_13]; the poor-season result bundles reduced tillage with residue retention [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_3]; the over-100% figure comes from purposely selected best-practice projects [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_15]; and the long-term trials are mainly from North America, Australia and Europe [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_16]. Readings in that review that misread their primaries were dropped, and the primaries themselves are now in the pool directly. Those best-practice arms are bundled: planting pits, basins or ripper-with-ridging (the capture element, which is the practice here) come with reduced tillage and mostly with fertiliser, and tillage alone is not water harvesting [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. The trial-level readings are weaker: the authors find no clear tillage effect on rain water productivity in Kenya, no clear effects of tillage in Ethiopia (where the gains that do show come with fertilised treatments), and only a tendency of improvement in semi-arid Tanzania [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_4]. The Burkina Faso trial covers the 2014 season only, and every conservation arm also received manure, so its gains belong to the package rather than to the structures alone [ev_crop_yield_koro17_1, ev_crop_yield_koro17_7]. At Houndé, grass strips with zaï (3507 kg per hectare with NPK and urea, 3065 kg averaged, against 2157 kg) were not significantly different from the control in yield, nor in rain water productivity (4.84 against 3.10) [ev_crop_yield_koro17_2, ev_crop_yield_koro17_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_2]. At Péni no conservation arm differed significantly from the control in yield or water productivity, grass strips with zaï giving 4192 kg and earth bunds with contour ploughing 4067 kg against 3317 kg per hectare; the authors attribute this to rainfall, saying water was not a limiting factor at Péni [ev_crop_yield_koro17_5, ev_crop_yield_koro17_6, ev_crop_yield_koro17_7, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_4]. The Sudan comparison ranks treatments without a no-practice value [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. These are compiler and author judgements across groups, direction only, and the review sentence is second-hand; the WOCAT authors also note that some case studies indicate little to no improvement in water use efficiency [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock10_1]. The FAO and WOCAT group marks are compiler judgements, direction only, and the conservation agriculture group bundles mulch with minimum tillage and rotation [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_4].

justification.mechanism: Water harvesting and conservation structures capture runoff and raise soil moisture so rainfed crops yield more, especially in dry years and low-rainfall areas; stored water allows supplemental irrigation and extra crops, and sediment and organic matter trapped behind structures add fertility. Meta-analyses now carry much of the evidence: A meta-analysis of traditional in-situ water harvesting finds a pooled yield gain of 71% over controls, with 142% for infiltration pits, 91% for mulching, 69% for soil and stone bunds, 48% for terraces and 74% for tied ridging [ev_crop_yield_tefe24_1, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_2, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_3, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_4, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_5, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_6]; a synthesis of Ethiopian studies gives mean grain-yield differences of 322 kg per hectare for stone bunds, 554.3 for tied ridges and 629.2 for mulching [ev_crop_yield_adim16_1, ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_4]; a sub-Saharan conservation agriculture meta-analysis finds yields 3.7% above conventional tillage overall, 8.4% for maize when all three principles are applied and 12.5% at sites with under 400 mm of seasonal rainfall, with the gain growing slowly over time [ev_crop_yield_corb20_1, ev_crop_yield_corb20_4, ev_crop_yield_corb20_6, ev_crop_yield_corb20_10]; and a terracing meta-analysis finds biomass on terraces about 1.94 times that on slopes, and reviewed studies report terraced teff, barley and maize yields at least two times those on slopes and 20% gains on young bench terraces in Peru [ev_crop_yield_wei16_1, ev_crop_yield_wei16_2, ev_crop_yield_wei16_4]. In Burkina Faso stone bunds raised sorghum yields by 33% to 55% and by about 142% with compost, on-farm trials in Mozambique gave maize gains of 504 to 800 kg per hectare on planting basins and direct-seeded plots, in Malawi's El Niño season ground cover raised maize from 247 to 432 kg per hectare, and silt farmland behind check dams on China's Loess Plateau yields 6–10 times more than sloping farmland [ev_crop_yield_zoug14_2, ev_crop_yield_zoug14_4, ev_crop_yield_thierf15_3, ev_crop_yield_boil19_2, ev_crop_yield_luca21_1]. Stored water stabilises output: Indian farmers reported crop-failure chances falling from 20% to 6% in the rainy season and from 100% to 5–10% in winter with a farm pond, sand dams cut crop failure against a control catchment in Kenya, and WOCAT compilers across many technology sheets judge crop, fodder and animal production increased [ev_yield_stability_pals23_1, ev_yield_stability_pals23_2, ev_crop_yield_lasage08_1]. In a Zimbabwe enterprise budget first-year planting-basin conservation farming yielded 1520 kg of maize per hectare against 400 kg on the fertilised conventional arm [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_2]. Newer field trials point the same way: In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, maize stalk mulch raised maize yield over no mulch at both sites in both seasons, and planting basins did so in 2012 [ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_1, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_2, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_3, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_4, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_6, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_8]. In Rwanda, vetiver mulch raised maize to 8089 kg per hectare against 4755 on flat rainfed plots [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_1], and in the same trial runoff from the terrace waterways, collected in a dug, lined pond and applied by a gravity drip kit as supplementary irrigation, gave 11982 kg per hectare [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_3]. In Burkina Faso, crop yields in years of average rainfall rose by 63–74 per cent on farms using rock bunds and by over 100 per cent on farms using zaï [ev_crop_yield_sawa11h1_1, ev_crop_yield_sawa11h1_2]. On crusted degraded soil in Burkina Faso, 30-cm zaï and 1-m half-moons with compost gave 408 and 1372 kg of millet per hectare where direct seeding gave none [ev_crop_yield_zour25h1_1, ev_crop_yield_zour25h1_2]. In Zimbabwe's El Niño drought season, maize under no-till with a residue mulch yielded 31.8% more than under conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_mash25h1_1]. A review cites soil and water conservation structures combined with biological measures raising wheat production by 30–45% over business-as-usual [ev_crop_yield_tade23h1_2]. Soils on Burkina Faso farms using soil and water conservation techniques had higher nitrogen contents than the control farm, used here as a component [ev_soil_nitrogen_sawa11h1_4]. Primary trials and surveys from eastern and southern Africa now stand in for second-hand Zambia readings. In on-farm trials in Ethiopia, ripper plus tied ridging with fertiliser gave 1775 kg of maize per hectare against 1458 under conventional maresha ploughing with the same fertiliser, and 1076 against 945 kg of tef [ev_crop_yield_rock09_1, ev_crop_yield_rock09_4]; in Tanzania, ripping and pitting combined with fertilisation gave yields 1.5–2.2 times those of conventional ploughing with the same fertilisation [ev_crop_yield_rock09_11]; and at Chipata, Zambia, basins with fertiliser gave 6660 kg of maize per hectare against 3153 under conventional practice [ev_crop_yield_rock09_13]. In Zambia's 2001/2 season hand-hoe conservation-farming basins gave 3,054 kg of maize per hectare against 1,339 under ploughing, and a regression controlling for planting date, hybrid seed and fertiliser puts the gain from the basins themselves closer to 700 kg per hectare for maize and 400 to 500 kg for cotton [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_2, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_3]; a later survey of Zambian conservation-agriculture households reports 5.2 t of maize per hectare in basins against 1.8 under the hand hoe [ev_crop_yield_umar11_1]. A meta-analysis of tied-ridge-furrow experiments finds tied ridges without fertiliser or mulch yielded 17% more sorghum grain than flat planting [ev_crop_yield_makm21_1]. In Madagascar, rice sown without tillage on a dead mulch and rotated averaged 2.8 against 2.6 t per hectare on lowland and 2.4 against 2.1 on hillside fields, and year-to-year variability fell after consecutive years under the system (a 6% and a 13% decrease in the coefficient of variation) [ev_crop_yield_brue14_1, ev_crop_yield_brue14_2, ev_yield_stability_brue14_3, ev_yield_stability_brue14_4]. Crop-model (APSIM) runs on semi-arid Zimbabwe weather give higher maize yields under conservation agriculture than under ploughing when aggregated across seasons, and more stable yields across different types of seasons [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_5, ev_yield_stability_faocr11_6]. In a Zimbabwe household panel, conservation agriculture (mostly planting basins, with residue mulch and rotation on some plots) improved maize yields both when rainfall was above average and during times of drought, and sorghum and cowpea yields during drought [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3, ev_crop_yield_mich19_4, ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. A review of conservation agriculture in Zambia also cites planting basins plus lime raising yields by 68% [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_1], a simulated gain of around 40% for the whole conservation farming package [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_6], higher soil moisture improving yields in poor seasons [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_3], and global syntheses: reduced tillage and crop residue management associated with a 106% increase in cereal yields, an average yield improvement of over 100% for smallholder conservation agriculture across 286 developing-country case studies, and a slight increase over conventional tillage, growing over time and especially in dry conditions, across 25 long-term trials [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_13, ev_crop_yield_arsl15_15, ev_crop_yield_arsl15_16]. Grain per unit of rain rises with capture in a set of East and Southern African trials: the best conservation-farming practice per site gave yield increases ranging from 20 to 120% over conventional tillage whilst rain water productivity improved with 10–50% [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. In an on-farm trial at Houndé, Burkina Faso, stone rows with zaï pits, every arm also receiving manure, raised maize grain to 4457 kg per hectare with NPK and urea against 2157 kg under the farmers' practice of oxen ploughing with NPK and urea, and to 3768 kg averaged over the fertility options, and lifted rain water productivity from 3.10 to 6.61 kg per hectare per mm [ev_crop_yield_koro17_1, ev_crop_yield_koro17_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_1]. A review reports that contour tied-ridging in eastern Sudan gave the highest water use efficiency of the treatments compared [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. The water-productivity evidence points the same way: FAO compilers list improved water use efficiency among the main benefits of rainwater harvesting, the WOCAT guideline authors find that all water harvesting groups indicate improved water use efficiency, mostly high to medium, through reduced evaporation loss and better soil water availability, and a review sentence, citing earlier work, says capture approaches often lead also to higher water productivity because denser canopies shade the soil [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock10_1]. The FAO compilers rate improving water productivity at the top of their scale for the conservation agriculture group [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_2]. They rate improving water productivity for the cross-slope barrier group at the middle mark of their scale [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_3]. For the WOCAT water harvesting groups the guideline authors' marks for improving water productivity run from the lowest positive mark for floodwater and microcatchment harvesting to the middle mark for macrocatchment harvesting [ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_3].
justification.conditionality: Held out of the class, as a caveat on where the practice performs rather than as production evidence: where rainfall is heavy the practice can lower yields through waterlogging, and the authors say so. Annual rainfall above 1000 mm affected the performance of Ethiopian soil and water conservation practices negatively, which the synthesis puts down to water logging on the furrows of structures, and fanya juu and soil bunds were associated with yield losses of 54 to 193 kg per hectare [ev_crop_yield_adim16_6, ev_crop_yield_adim16_2]; plots with bunds yielded less than non-conserved plots in high-rainfall western Amhara [ev_crop_yield_schmidt12_10]; in the Sudanian zone of Cameroon, where rain exceeds 80 mm a day and 1,200 mm a year, sorghum in zaï pits yielded less than flat-cultivated fields because of frequent waterlogging and the risk of nutrient leaching [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]; 92% of the data in a conservation agriculture review show mulch cover in high-rainfall areas lowering yields through waterlogging [ev_crop_yield_rusin11_3]; and at sites with over 1,200 mm of seasonal rainfall conservation agriculture yielded 4.3% less than conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_corb20_7]. In a wetter sub-humid Kenyan site, ridged plots with fertiliser gave the lowest yields, slightly below conventional practice, which the authors say can probably be explained by waterlogging caused by ridging [ev_crop_yield_rock09_6]. Read these as a siting limit: the practice should not be applied where rainfall is that heavy. Other measured losses do count against the class: bunds cut yields by up to 7% in the first few years in Ethiopia, and stone bunds in semi-arid Tanzania reduced maize yield by 13% [ev_crop_yield_adim16_7, ev_crop_yield_adim16_9]. The sub-Saharan conservation agriculture meta-analysis finds no significant gain for crops other than maize, and outperformance of conventional tillage only with no-tillage systems rather than planting basins or minimum tillage [ev_crop_yield_corb20_3, ev_crop_yield_corb20_9]; a maize meta-regression finds conservation agriculture consistently underperforms on high-clay soils in very wet seasons, though at median rainfall and clay it outperforms conventional practice even without fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_stew18_3, ev_crop_yield_stew18_4]; and in drought seasons in Mozambique and Zimbabwe conservation agriculture gave no harvest or yielded less than conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_thierf15_1, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_7]. In Algeria farmers lost 5 to 15% of their cropped area to banquettes without seeing yields improve, legume yields between banquettes showed no significant gain, and a Moroccan farmer saw no yield improvement between banquettes imposed by technicians [ev_crop_yield_arab04_1, ev_crop_yield_arab04_2, ev_crop_yield_roos10_2]. Other nulls and negatives: conservation promoted mostly off-farm had no yield effect, benefits in Ethiopia appeared only once structures were maintained for at least seven years, diversion banquettes in Niger cut yields, and soil salinisation can appear on check-dam farmland [ev_crop_yield_luca21_1]. Outside the meta-analyses the pool mixes independent evaluations with lender completion-report figures, bundled watershed programmes, reviews quoting ranges from earlier studies, a farmer survey reported in a preprint and many practitioner judgements; much of the zai and planting-basin gain rides on added manure, compost or fertiliser [ev_yield_stability_pals23_1, ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1]. In the Malawi El Nino survey banking, the reinforcement of ridges while the crop is growing, cut maize from 245 to 153 kg per hectare, so some in-field practices lowered yield in that season [ev_crop_yield_boil19_5]. Planting basins gave no significant gain over no mulch in 2011 at either Ethiopian site (4239 against 4171 and 4265 against 4131 kg per hectare) [ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_5, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_7]. Rwandan contour ridges were not significantly different from flat rainfed plots (5937 against 4755 kg per hectare) [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_2]. The Burkina Faso zaï and half-moon contrasts are against land where direct seeding produced no grain, with compost added to the pits, so they measure bringing degraded land into production rather than an improvement on a cropped field. The Burkina Faso farm gains are for years the authors call average rainfall, with compost on the bunded fields. The Zimbabwe residue-mulch gain is one on-station season with no normal-year comparison, and the mulch is bundled with no-till [ev_crop_yield_mash25h1_1]. The wheat figure is a review's citation of a package that includes biological measures [ev_crop_yield_tade23h1_2]. The Rwandan pond result is a bundle — terrace runoff capture, a lined storage pond and drip irrigation — so the yield is delivered through irrigation hardware and cannot be read as a pure capture effect; it is one season of a randomised trial in which every plot received farmyard manure and mineral fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_3]. The East African and Zambian trial gains are bundles. In Ethiopia the comparator carried the same fertiliser, but without fertiliser neither improved tillage nor fertiliser alone raised maize significantly, and the 20–50% tef gain without fertiliser was not significant [ev_crop_yield_rock09_2, ev_crop_yield_rock09_3]; the Tanzanian ripping-or-pitting arms are bundled with reduced tillage [ev_crop_yield_rock09_11]; and the Chipata basins carried improved seed against a conventional practice with extremely low fertiliser, in seasons of well-above-average rainfall, a gain the authors say cannot be fully explained [ev_crop_yield_rock09_13]. Some trial arms lost: pitting with fertiliser was the lowest-yielding treatment at Machakos, at 1.2 against 1.6 t per hectare under conventional practice [ev_crop_yield_rock09_9], and at the more arid Kenyan sites each site recorded complete crop failures in two out of three and four seasons, which the treatments did not avert; water harvesting is not irrigation [ev_crop_yield_rock09_10]. The Zambian 2001/2 raw contrast is one season with no normal-year reference and mixes the basin effect with higher input use, since most basin farmers received hybrid seed, fertiliser and lime on credit; the regression figure is the cleaner estimate, and even its basin dummy also picks up extra weeding labour and lime [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_2]. The later Zambian survey yields are farmer self-reports with large spreads, and the basin gain over ploughing (5.2 against 3.8 t per hectare) was not significant [ev_crop_yield_umar11_1, ev_crop_yield_umar11_2]; a national Zambian smallholder panel finds no significant maize yield effect of planting basins under any of its estimators [ev_crop_yield_burk12_1]; and paired soil samples on Zambian fields under basins or ripping (bundled with reduced tillage), with residues hardly retained, showed no significant difference in nitrogen [ev_soil_nitrogen_umar11_6]. The Zimbabwe panel keeps drought-season and normal-season results apart: in average rainfall periods conservation agriculture had no significant impact on any crop, in another specification it decreased maize yields by itself, and it did not mitigate rainfall-shortfall or surplus losses for millet and groundnut, so its gains appear only in seasons away from the average [ev_crop_yield_mich19_1, ev_crop_yield_mich19_2, ev_crop_yield_mich19_6, ev_crop_yield_mich19_7]. The tied-ridge meta-analysis finds no significant millet gain over flat planting and no significant difference when grass mulch was added to the ridges, and its sorghum observation count is internally inconsistent [ev_crop_yield_makm21_3, ev_crop_yield_makm21_2, ev_crop_yield_makm21_1]. In Madagascar the severe drought of 2007–2008 could not be offset by the system, and the pooled comparison showed no change in yield variance, the stability gain appearing only after consecutive years; the rice gains bundle no-till, mulch and rotation [ev_crop_yield_brue14_5, ev_yield_stability_brue14_7]. The crop-model results are simulations that bundle residue cover, better infiltration and fertiliser targeting; under sub-humid weather the model gives no difference [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_4], and in seasons with 230 mm and 176 mm of in-crop rainfall there was total crop failure under both systems [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_2]. Farmer reports of basin yields of >1 tonnes per hectare in poor-rainfall seasons, against total failure under ploughing, compare fertilised basins with unfertilised ploughing, which the author calls too confounded [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_9]. The remaining Zambia and global figures are cited secondhand in Arslan and colleagues' literature review, and none has a normal-year comparison: the 68% gain is for planting basins plus lime application, with timely conventional farming giving 50% in the same trials [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_1]; the roughly 40% gain is a simulation of the whole conservation farming package, through early planting and improved soil quality [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_6]; the 106% is for reduced tillage together with residue management [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_13]; the poor-season result bundles reduced tillage with residue retention [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_3]; the over-100% figure comes from purposely selected best-practice projects [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_15]; and the long-term trials are mainly from North America, Australia and Europe [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_16]. Readings in that review that misread their primaries were dropped, and the primaries themselves are now in the pool directly. Those best-practice arms are bundled: planting pits, basins or ripper-with-ridging (the capture element, which is the practice here) come with reduced tillage and mostly with fertiliser, and tillage alone is not water harvesting [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. The trial-level readings are weaker: the authors find no clear tillage effect on rain water productivity in Kenya, no clear effects of tillage in Ethiopia (where the gains that do show come with fertilised treatments), and only a tendency of improvement in semi-arid Tanzania [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_4]. The Burkina Faso trial covers the 2014 season only, and every conservation arm also received manure, so its gains belong to the package rather than to the structures alone [ev_crop_yield_koro17_1, ev_crop_yield_koro17_7]. At Houndé, grass strips with zaï (3507 kg per hectare with NPK and urea, 3065 kg averaged, against 2157 kg) were not significantly different from the control in yield, nor in rain water productivity (4.84 against 3.10) [ev_crop_yield_koro17_2, ev_crop_yield_koro17_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_2]. At Péni no conservation arm differed significantly from the control in yield or water productivity, grass strips with zaï giving 4192 kg and earth bunds with contour ploughing 4067 kg against 3317 kg per hectare; the authors attribute this to rainfall, saying water was not a limiting factor at Péni [ev_crop_yield_koro17_5, ev_crop_yield_koro17_6, ev_crop_yield_koro17_7, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_4]. The Sudan comparison ranks treatments without a no-practice value [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. These are compiler and author judgements across groups, direction only, and the review sentence is second-hand; the WOCAT authors also note that some case studies indicate little to no improvement in water use efficiency [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock10_1]. The FAO and WOCAT group marks are compiler judgements, direction only, and the conservation agriculture group bundles mulch with minimum tillage and rotation [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_4].

effect_mechanism: In the tropical highlands, soil and water conservation has measured yield gains and measured yield losses, depending on the practice. Gains: an Ethiopian synthesis finds mean grain-yield gains of 322 kg per hectare for stone bunds, 554.3 for tied ridges and 629.2 for mulching, stone and soil bunds raising yields by up to 10% in Tigray, and stone bunds raising soil total nitrogen from 0.16 to 0.20% [ev_crop_yield_adim16_1, ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_4, ev_crop_yield_adim16_8, ev_soil_nitrogen_adim16_1]; in a Kenyan highland trial, tied ridges in long rains with dry spells gave 4.10 against 3.15 t of maize per hectare with manure and fertiliser, and 2.53 against 1.82 t without inputs (not significant), and tended to give less variable yields [ev_crop_yield_ndun23_3, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_1, ev_yield_stability_ndun23_1]; in Peru, 2 to 4-year old bench terraces gave 20% greater yields than adjacent sloping fields [ev_crop_yield_wei16_4]. Losses: in the same Ethiopian synthesis fanya juu and soil bunds were associated with yield losses of 54 to 193 kg per hectare, bunds cut yields by up to 7% in the first few years, and annual rainfall above 1000 mm affected performance negatively, which the authors suggest may be waterlogging in the furrows of structures [ev_crop_yield_adim16_2, ev_crop_yield_adim16_7, ev_crop_yield_adim16_6].
conditionality: The class is set by the gains. The fanya juu and soil bund losses and the finding that annual rainfall above 1000 mm affected performance negatively are held out of it, because the synthesis puts that effect down to excessive water availability (water logging) on the furrows of structures [ev_crop_yield_adim16_2, ev_crop_yield_adim16_6]: they are logged as a performance caveat — these structures should not be applied where rainfall is that heavy — rather than as production evidence. The evidence points to three things that separate gains from losses. Practice type: stone bunds, tied ridges and mulching gained, while graded and level fanya juu, soil bunds and grass strips lost yield in the Ethiopian table [ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_2]. Rainfall: the gaining practices were studied at lower average rainfall (695.1 mm for tied ridges, 876.7 mm for mulching) than the losing bunds (1030.2 to 1454.3 mm), and rainfall above 1000 mm reduced performance [ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_6]; practice and rainfall travel together in that table, so the two cannot be fully separated. Time: bunds lose yield in the first few years [ev_crop_yield_adim16_7]. For a Task Team Leader the actionable reading is to match the structure to the rainfall regime, favouring in-field moisture capture in drier highlands and avoiding fanya juu and soil bunds where waterlogging is likely, and to budget for an early yield dip. At the dry end, tied ridging gave no advantage in the Kenyan short rains with meteorological droughts, since there was little rain to hold [ev_crop_yield_ndun23_2, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_4, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_5]. On quality, both sides rest mainly on the same Ethiopian synthesis of unweighted means pooled across studies; the Kenyan result is a single-site trial whose lower-variability finding was not tested, and the Peruvian figure is cited in a review [ev_crop_yield_adim16_1, ev_yield_stability_ndun23_1, ev_crop_yield_wei16_4].
