justification.mechanism: In the tropical highlands, soil and water conservation has measured yield gains and measured yield losses, depending on the practice. Gains: an Ethiopian synthesis finds mean grain-yield gains of 322 kg per hectare for stone bunds, 554.3 for tied ridges and 629.2 for mulching, stone and soil bunds raising yields by up to 10% in Tigray, and stone bunds raising soil total nitrogen from 0.16 to 0.20% [ev_crop_yield_adim16_1, ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_4, ev_crop_yield_adim16_8, ev_soil_nitrogen_adim16_1]; in a Kenyan highland trial, tied ridges in long rains with dry spells gave 4.10 against 3.15 t of maize per hectare with manure and fertiliser, and 2.53 against 1.82 t without inputs (not significant), and tended to give less variable yields [ev_crop_yield_ndun23_3, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_1, ev_yield_stability_ndun23_1]; in Peru, 2 to 4-year old bench terraces gave 20% greater yields than adjacent sloping fields [ev_crop_yield_wei16_4]. Losses: in the same Ethiopian synthesis fanya juu and soil bunds were associated with yield losses of 54 to 193 kg per hectare, bunds cut yields by up to 7% in the first few years, and annual rainfall above 1000 mm affected performance negatively, which the authors suggest may be waterlogging in the furrows of structures [ev_crop_yield_adim16_2, ev_crop_yield_adim16_7, ev_crop_yield_adim16_6].
justification.conditionality: The class is set by the gains. The fanya juu and soil bund losses and the finding that annual rainfall above 1000 mm affected performance negatively are held out of it, because the synthesis puts that effect down to excessive water availability (water logging) on the furrows of structures [ev_crop_yield_adim16_2, ev_crop_yield_adim16_6]: they are logged as a performance caveat — these structures should not be applied where rainfall is that heavy — rather than as production evidence. The evidence points to three things that separate gains from losses. Practice type: stone bunds, tied ridges and mulching gained, while graded and level fanya juu, soil bunds and grass strips lost yield in the Ethiopian table [ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_2]. Rainfall: the gaining practices were studied at lower average rainfall (695.1 mm for tied ridges, 876.7 mm for mulching) than the losing bunds (1030.2 to 1454.3 mm), and rainfall above 1000 mm reduced performance [ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_6]; practice and rainfall travel together in that table, so the two cannot be fully separated. Time: bunds lose yield in the first few years [ev_crop_yield_adim16_7]. For a Task Team Leader the actionable reading is to match the structure to the rainfall regime, favouring in-field moisture capture in drier highlands and avoiding fanya juu and soil bunds where waterlogging is likely, and to budget for an early yield dip. At the dry end, tied ridging gave no advantage in the Kenyan short rains with meteorological droughts, since there was little rain to hold [ev_crop_yield_ndun23_2, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_4, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_5]. On quality, both sides rest mainly on the same Ethiopian synthesis of unweighted means pooled across studies; the Kenyan result is a single-site trial whose lower-variability finding was not tested, and the Peruvian figure is cited in a review [ev_crop_yield_adim16_1, ev_yield_stability_ndun23_1, ev_crop_yield_wei16_4].

effect_mechanism: Soil and water conservation and water harvesting have been found both to raise and to lower production. Gains come from retaining moisture and soil: a meta-analysis of traditional in-situ water harvesting finds a pooled yield gain of 71% over controls, with 69% for soil and stone bunds and gains of 71.7% for maize and 68.2% for sorghum without fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_tefe24_1, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_4, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_7, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_8]; four studies in a systematic review find 20–24 per cent gains in crop yield or value of production, particularly in regions with low rainfall or high climatic variability [ev_crop_yield_mala24_1, ev_crop_yield_mala24_3, ev_crop_yield_mala24_5]; zai pits combined with stone lines in Burkina Faso are reported to raise sorghum yields by over 100% [ev_crop_yield_ngur26_3]; Ethiopian early adopters had a 15.2 percent higher value of production and invested plots 20.6 percent higher [ev_agricultural_production_value_schmidt12_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_schmidt12_4]; physical structures buffered crop growth against the 2015 severe drought in Ethiopia [ev_crop_yield_meaza22_1]; and dry spells can be bridged through water management [ev_crop_yield_rock10_1]. Programme reports add rainfed yield gains of 24% to 26% in Karnataka and 20.8% in Uttarakhand, yields rising from 0.5 to more than 1.2 t per hectare in wetter Mauritanian watersheds, and crop diversification from water harvesting with irrigation [ev_crop_yield_iegind11_1, ev_crop_yield_utk22_1, ev_crop_yield_mrt14_2, ev_agricultural_production_value_arega24_2]. Losses come from structures taking cropland and from excess water: in an Ethiopian synthesis fanya juu and soil bunds were associated with yield losses of 54 to 193 kg per hectare, bunds cut yields by up to 7% in the first few years, and rainfall above 1000 mm affected performance negatively, possibly through waterlogging [ev_crop_yield_adim16_2, ev_crop_yield_adim16_7, ev_crop_yield_adim16_6]; plots with bunds yielded less than non-conserved plots in high-rainfall western Amhara [ev_crop_yield_schmidt12_10]. A review cites soil and water conservation structures combined with biological measures raising wheat production by 30–45% over business-as-usual [ev_crop_yield_tade23h1_2]. Soils on Burkina Faso farms using soil and water conservation techniques had higher nitrogen contents than the control farm, used here as a component [ev_soil_nitrogen_sawa11h1_4]. The water-productivity evidence points the same way: FAO compilers list improved water use efficiency among the main benefits of rainwater harvesting, the WOCAT guideline authors find that all water harvesting groups indicate improved water use efficiency, mostly high to medium, through reduced evaporation loss and better soil water availability, and a review sentence, citing earlier work, says capture approaches often lead also to higher water productivity because denser canopies shade the soil [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock10_1].
conditionality: The class is set by the gains. The excess-water losses are held out of it as a caveat on where the practice performs rather than as production evidence: annual rainfall above 1000 mm affected performance negatively, which the synthesis puts down to water logging on the furrows of structures, fanya juu and soil bunds were associated with yield losses of 54 to 193 kg per hectare, and plots with bunds yielded less than non-conserved plots in high-rainfall western Amhara [ev_crop_yield_adim16_6, ev_crop_yield_adim16_2, ev_crop_yield_schmidt12_10]. Bunds should not be applied where rainfall is that heavy. The evidence itself names what separates gains from losses. Rainfall: gains concentrate in low-rainfall or variable areas and in drier periods, while bunds lose yield in high-rainfall areas, and in Tigray bunds slightly raised productivity in drier periods but reduced it in moist seasons because cropped area was lost to the bunds [ev_crop_yield_mala24_3, ev_crop_yield_schmidt12_10, ev_crop_yield_schmidt12_8, ev_crop_yield_adim16_6]. Time and maintenance: value of production rose only after structures had been maintained for at least 7 years, later adopters saw no significant gain, and bunds cut yields in the first few years [ev_agricultural_production_value_schmidt12_5, ev_agricultural_production_value_schmidt12_2, ev_crop_yield_adim16_7]. Who decides: imposed structures often reduced cultivable area by 3 to 20% without improving productivity, and structures promoted mostly off-farm for community resource protection gave no gain [ev_crop_yield_roose94_5, ev_crop_yield_abate21_1]. Severity: dry spells can be bridged but yields cannot be sustained in a meteorological drought [ev_crop_yield_rock10_2]. Practice: fanya juu and soil bunds account for the measured losses [ev_crop_yield_adim16_2]. The actionable distinctions are therefore siting by rainfall regime, farmer-owned rather than imposed structures, and a maintenance horizon of years. On quality, many of the largest gains are from bundled programmes or lender completion reports (Ethiopia public works, India watershed projects, Mauritania), with value of production and forage biomass used as proxies, while the losses come from an Ethiopian synthesis and a matched study; the drought finding is a secondary citation in a review [ev_crop_yield_utk22_1, ev_crop_yield_mrt14_2, ev_forage_productivity_mrt14_3, ev_crop_yield_meaza22_1]. The wheat figure is a review's citation of a package that includes biological measures [ev_crop_yield_tade23h1_2]. The nitrogen finding is a content on farm soils, not a yield [ev_soil_nitrogen_sawa11h1_4]. These are compiler and author judgements across groups, direction only, and the review sentence is second-hand; the WOCAT authors also note that some case studies indicate little to no improvement in water use efficiency [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock10_1].

effect_mechanism: Planting pits (zai, tassa), tied ridges and furrows, mulch, basin tillage and infiltration trenches capture runoff near the plants; combined with manure they let cereals be grown on degraded crusted soils, and in the 1990 drought in Niger only tassa fields produced a harvest. Meta-analyses quantify the gain: a meta-analysis of traditional in-situ water harvesting finds yield increases of 142% for infiltration pits, 91% for mulching and 74% for tied ridging over controls [ev_crop_yield_tefe24_2, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_3, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_6]; a synthesis of Ethiopian studies gives mean grain-yield differences of 554.3 kg per hectare for tied ridges and 629.2 for mulching [ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_4]; a sub-Saharan conservation agriculture meta-analysis finds yields 3.7% above conventional tillage overall, 8.4% for maize when all three principles are applied and 12.5% at sites with under 400 mm of seasonal rainfall, with the gain growing slowly over time [ev_crop_yield_corb20_1, ev_crop_yield_corb20_4, ev_crop_yield_corb20_6, ev_crop_yield_corb20_10]; a maize meta-regression finds conservation agriculture outperforms conventional practice at median rainfall and clay even without fertiliser and gains more as seasons get drier [ev_crop_yield_stew18_4, ev_crop_yield_stew18_1]; and earlier meta-analyses find no-till with residue retention and rotation raises rainfed yields by 7.3% in dry climates [ev_crop_yield_pittel15_2]. On farms, ground cover raised maize from 247 to 432 kg per hectare in Malawi's El Niño season, first-year planting-basin farmers in Zimbabwe obtained 1520 kg against 368 kg per hectare, tied ridges raised maize significantly in Tanzania, review ranges for zai and tassa pits run to 100–200% yield gains, and planting basins and direct seeding in Mozambique gave maize gains of 504 to 800 kg per hectare [ev_crop_yield_boil19_2, ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_6, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_1, ev_crop_yield_thierf15_3]; WOCAT compilers for pits, contour bunds and conservation tillage in several countries judge crop production increased. In a Zimbabwe enterprise budget first-year planting-basin conservation farming yielded 1520 kg of maize per hectare against 400 kg on the fertilised conventional arm [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_2]. Newer field trials add: In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, maize stalk mulch raised maize yield over no mulch at both sites in both seasons, and planting basins did so in 2012 [ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_1, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_2, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_3, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_4, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_6, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_8]. In Rwanda, vetiver mulch raised maize to 8089 kg per hectare against 4755 on flat rainfed plots [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_1]. In Burkina Faso, crop yields in years of average rainfall rose by over 100 per cent on farms using zaï [ev_crop_yield_sawa11h1_1]. On crusted degraded soil in Burkina Faso, 30-cm zaï with compost gave 408 kg of millet per hectare where direct seeding gave none [ev_crop_yield_zour25h1_1]. In Zimbabwe's El Niño drought season, maize under no-till with a residue mulch yielded 31.8% more than under conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_mash25h1_1]. Primary trials and surveys from eastern and southern Africa now stand in for second-hand Zambia readings. In on-farm trials in Ethiopia, ripper plus tied ridging with fertiliser gave 1775 kg of maize per hectare against 1458 under conventional maresha ploughing with the same fertiliser, and 1076 against 945 kg of tef [ev_crop_yield_rock09_1, ev_crop_yield_rock09_4]; in Tanzania, ripping and pitting combined with fertilisation gave yields 1.5–2.2 times those of conventional ploughing with the same fertilisation [ev_crop_yield_rock09_11]; and at Chipata, Zambia, basins with fertiliser gave 6660 kg of maize per hectare against 3153 under conventional practice [ev_crop_yield_rock09_13]. In Zambia's 2001/2 season hand-hoe conservation-farming basins gave 3,054 kg of maize per hectare against 1,339 under ploughing, and a regression controlling for planting date, hybrid seed and fertiliser puts the gain from the basins themselves closer to 700 kg per hectare for maize and 400 to 500 kg for cotton [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_2, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_3]; a later survey of Zambian conservation-agriculture households reports 5.2 t of maize per hectare in basins against 1.8 under the hand hoe [ev_crop_yield_umar11_1]. A meta-analysis of tied-ridge-furrow experiments finds tied ridges without fertiliser or mulch yielded 17% more sorghum grain than flat planting [ev_crop_yield_makm21_1]. In Madagascar, rice sown without tillage on a dead mulch and rotated averaged 2.8 against 2.6 t per hectare on lowland and 2.4 against 2.1 on hillside fields, and year-to-year variability fell after consecutive years under the system (a 6% and a 13% decrease in the coefficient of variation) [ev_crop_yield_brue14_1, ev_crop_yield_brue14_2, ev_yield_stability_brue14_3, ev_yield_stability_brue14_4]. Crop-model (APSIM) runs on semi-arid Zimbabwe weather give higher maize yields under conservation agriculture than under ploughing when aggregated across seasons, and more stable yields across different types of seasons [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_5, ev_yield_stability_faocr11_6]. In a Zimbabwe household panel, conservation agriculture (mostly planting basins, with residue mulch and rotation on some plots) improved maize yields both when rainfall was above average and during times of drought, and sorghum and cowpea yields during drought [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3, ev_crop_yield_mich19_4, ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. A review of conservation agriculture in Zambia also cites planting basins plus lime raising yields by 68% [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_1], a simulated gain of around 40% for the whole conservation farming package [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_6], higher soil moisture improving yields in poor seasons [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_3], and global syntheses: reduced tillage and crop residue management associated with a 106% increase in cereal yields, an average yield improvement of over 100% for smallholder conservation agriculture across 286 developing-country case studies, and a slight increase over conventional tillage, growing over time and especially in dry conditions, across 25 long-term trials [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_13, ev_crop_yield_arsl15_15, ev_crop_yield_arsl15_16]. Grain per unit of rain rises with capture in a set of East and Southern African trials: the best conservation-farming practice per site gave yield increases ranging from 20 to 120% over conventional tillage whilst rain water productivity improved with 10–50% [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. In an on-farm trial at Houndé, Burkina Faso, stone rows with zaï pits, every arm also receiving manure, raised maize grain to 4457 kg per hectare with NPK and urea against 2157 kg under the farmers' practice of oxen ploughing with NPK and urea, and to 3768 kg averaged over the fertility options, and lifted rain water productivity from 3.10 to 6.61 kg per hectare per mm [ev_crop_yield_koro17_1, ev_crop_yield_koro17_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_1]. A review reports that contour tied-ridging in eastern Sudan gave the highest water use efficiency of the treatments compared [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. The FAO compilers rate improving water productivity at the top of their scale for the conservation agriculture group [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_2].
conditionality: Held out of the class, as a caveat on where the practice performs rather than as production evidence: in the Sudanian zone of Cameroon, where rain exceeds 80 mm a day and 1,200 mm a year, sorghum in zaï pits yielded less than flat-cultivated fields because of frequent waterlogging and the risk of nutrient leaching [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]; 92% of the data in a conservation agriculture review show mulch cover in high-rainfall areas lowering yields through waterlogging [ev_crop_yield_rusin11_3]; and at sites with over 1,200 mm of seasonal rainfall conservation agriculture yielded 4.3% less than conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_corb20_7]. In a wetter sub-humid Kenyan site, ridged plots with fertiliser gave the lowest yields, slightly below conventional practice, which the authors say can probably be explained by waterlogging caused by ridging [ev_crop_yield_rock09_6]. Read these as a siting limit: in-situ capture should not be applied where rainfall is that heavy. In drought seasons gains vanish: conservation agriculture pillars had no detectable effect in a Kenyan season with a failed start, tied ridging gave no advantage in Kenyan short rains with meteorological droughts, and in Mozambique and Zimbabwe conservation agriculture gave no harvest or yielded less than conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_boil19_3, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_2, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_5, ev_crop_yield_thierf15_1, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_7]. Much of the pit gain depends on manure or fertiliser (pits alone gave an average sorghum gain of only 38 kg/ha in one study against 310 kg/ha in another), the Zimbabwe planting-basin gain also carries manure and fertiliser, and the review ranges for pits are not pooled estimates [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_1]. In the Malawi El Nino survey banking, the reinforcement of ridges while the crop is growing, cut maize from 245 to 153 kg per hectare, so some in-field practices lowered yield in that season [ev_crop_yield_boil19_5]. Planting basins gave no significant gain over no mulch in 2011 at either Ethiopian site (4239 against 4171 and 4265 against 4131 kg per hectare) [ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_5, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_7]. Rwandan contour ridges were not significantly different from flat rainfed plots (5937 against 4755 kg per hectare) [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_2]. The Burkina Faso zaï and half-moon contrasts are against land where direct seeding produced no grain, with compost added to the pits, so they measure bringing degraded land into production rather than an improvement on a cropped field. The Zimbabwe residue-mulch gain is one on-station season with no normal-year comparison, and the mulch is bundled with no-till [ev_crop_yield_mash25h1_1]. The East African and Zambian trial gains are bundles. In Ethiopia the comparator carried the same fertiliser, but without fertiliser neither improved tillage nor fertiliser alone raised maize significantly, and the 20–50% tef gain without fertiliser was not significant [ev_crop_yield_rock09_2, ev_crop_yield_rock09_3]; the Tanzanian ripping-or-pitting arms are bundled with reduced tillage [ev_crop_yield_rock09_11]; and the Chipata basins carried improved seed against a conventional practice with extremely low fertiliser, in seasons of well-above-average rainfall, a gain the authors say cannot be fully explained [ev_crop_yield_rock09_13]. Some trial arms lost: pitting with fertiliser was the lowest-yielding treatment at Machakos, at 1.2 against 1.6 t per hectare under conventional practice [ev_crop_yield_rock09_9], and at the more arid Kenyan sites each site recorded complete crop failures in two out of three and four seasons, which the treatments did not avert; water harvesting is not irrigation [ev_crop_yield_rock09_10]. The Zambian 2001/2 raw contrast is one season with no normal-year reference and mixes the basin effect with higher input use, since most basin farmers received hybrid seed, fertiliser and lime on credit; the regression figure is the cleaner estimate, and even its basin dummy also picks up extra weeding labour and lime [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_2]. The later Zambian survey yields are farmer self-reports with large spreads, and the basin gain over ploughing (5.2 against 3.8 t per hectare) was not significant [ev_crop_yield_umar11_1, ev_crop_yield_umar11_2]; a national Zambian smallholder panel finds no significant maize yield effect of planting basins under any of its estimators [ev_crop_yield_burk12_1]; and paired soil samples on Zambian fields under basins or ripping (bundled with reduced tillage), with residues hardly retained, showed no significant difference in nitrogen [ev_soil_nitrogen_umar11_6]. The Zimbabwe panel keeps drought-season and normal-season results apart: in average rainfall periods conservation agriculture had no significant impact on any crop, in another specification it decreased maize yields by itself, and it did not mitigate rainfall-shortfall or surplus losses for millet and groundnut, so its gains appear only in seasons away from the average [ev_crop_yield_mich19_1, ev_crop_yield_mich19_2, ev_crop_yield_mich19_6, ev_crop_yield_mich19_7]. The tied-ridge meta-analysis finds no significant millet gain over flat planting and no significant difference when grass mulch was added to the ridges, and its sorghum observation count is internally inconsistent [ev_crop_yield_makm21_3, ev_crop_yield_makm21_2, ev_crop_yield_makm21_1]. In Madagascar the severe drought of 2007–2008 could not be offset by the system, and the pooled comparison showed no change in yield variance, the stability gain appearing only after consecutive years; the rice gains bundle no-till, mulch and rotation [ev_crop_yield_brue14_5, ev_yield_stability_brue14_7]. The crop-model results are simulations that bundle residue cover, better infiltration and fertiliser targeting; under sub-humid weather the model gives no difference [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_4], and in seasons with 230 mm and 176 mm of in-crop rainfall there was total crop failure under both systems [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_2]. Farmer reports of basin yields of >1 tonnes per hectare in poor-rainfall seasons, against total failure under ploughing, compare fertilised basins with unfertilised ploughing, which the author calls too confounded [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_9]. The remaining Zambia and global figures are cited secondhand in Arslan and colleagues' literature review, and none has a normal-year comparison: the 68% gain is for planting basins plus lime application, with timely conventional farming giving 50% in the same trials [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_1]; the roughly 40% gain is a simulation of the whole conservation farming package, through early planting and improved soil quality [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_6]; the 106% is for reduced tillage together with residue management [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_13]; the poor-season result bundles reduced tillage with residue retention [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_3]; the over-100% figure comes from purposely selected best-practice projects [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_15]; and the long-term trials are mainly from North America, Australia and Europe [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_16]. Readings in that review that misread their primaries were dropped, and the primaries themselves are now in the pool directly. Those best-practice arms are bundled: planting pits, basins or ripper-with-ridging (the capture element, which is the practice here) come with reduced tillage and mostly with fertiliser, and tillage alone is not water harvesting [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. The trial-level readings are weaker: the authors find no clear tillage effect on rain water productivity in Kenya, no clear effects of tillage in Ethiopia (where the gains that do show come with fertilised treatments), and only a tendency of improvement in semi-arid Tanzania [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_4]. The Burkina Faso trial covers the 2014 season only, and every conservation arm also received manure, so its gains belong to the package rather than to the structures alone [ev_crop_yield_koro17_1, ev_crop_yield_koro17_7]. At Houndé, grass strips with zaï (3507 kg per hectare with NPK and urea, 3065 kg averaged, against 2157 kg) were not significantly different from the control in yield, nor in rain water productivity (4.84 against 3.10) [ev_crop_yield_koro17_2, ev_crop_yield_koro17_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_2]. At Péni no conservation arm differed significantly from the control in yield or water productivity, grass strips with zaï giving 4192 kg and earth bunds with contour ploughing 4067 kg against 3317 kg per hectare; the authors attribute this to rainfall, saying water was not a limiting factor at Péni [ev_crop_yield_koro17_5, ev_crop_yield_koro17_6, ev_crop_yield_koro17_7, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_4]. The Sudan comparison ranks treatments without a no-practice value [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. That rating is a compiler judgement for a group that bundles mulch with minimum tillage and rotation, so it does not isolate the soil-cover capture element [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_2].

justification.mechanism: Planting pits (zai, tassa), tied ridges and furrows, mulch, basin tillage and infiltration trenches capture runoff near the plants; combined with manure they let cereals be grown on degraded crusted soils, and in the 1990 drought in Niger only tassa fields produced a harvest. Meta-analyses quantify the gain: a meta-analysis of traditional in-situ water harvesting finds yield increases of 142% for infiltration pits, 91% for mulching and 74% for tied ridging over controls [ev_crop_yield_tefe24_2, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_3, ev_crop_yield_tefe24_6]; a synthesis of Ethiopian studies gives mean grain-yield differences of 554.3 kg per hectare for tied ridges and 629.2 for mulching [ev_crop_yield_adim16_3, ev_crop_yield_adim16_4]; a sub-Saharan conservation agriculture meta-analysis finds yields 3.7% above conventional tillage overall, 8.4% for maize when all three principles are applied and 12.5% at sites with under 400 mm of seasonal rainfall, with the gain growing slowly over time [ev_crop_yield_corb20_1, ev_crop_yield_corb20_4, ev_crop_yield_corb20_6, ev_crop_yield_corb20_10]; a maize meta-regression finds conservation agriculture outperforms conventional practice at median rainfall and clay even without fertiliser and gains more as seasons get drier [ev_crop_yield_stew18_4, ev_crop_yield_stew18_1]; and earlier meta-analyses find no-till with residue retention and rotation raises rainfed yields by 7.3% in dry climates [ev_crop_yield_pittel15_2]. On farms, ground cover raised maize from 247 to 432 kg per hectare in Malawi's El Niño season, first-year planting-basin farmers in Zimbabwe obtained 1520 kg against 368 kg per hectare, tied ridges raised maize significantly in Tanzania, review ranges for zai and tassa pits run to 100–200% yield gains, and planting basins and direct seeding in Mozambique gave maize gains of 504 to 800 kg per hectare [ev_crop_yield_boil19_2, ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_6, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_1, ev_crop_yield_thierf15_3]; WOCAT compilers for pits, contour bunds and conservation tillage in several countries judge crop production increased. In a Zimbabwe enterprise budget first-year planting-basin conservation farming yielded 1520 kg of maize per hectare against 400 kg on the fertilised conventional arm [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_2]. Newer field trials add: In an Ethiopian Rift Valley trial, maize stalk mulch raised maize yield over no mulch at both sites in both seasons, and planting basins did so in 2012 [ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_1, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_2, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_3, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_4, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_6, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_8]. In Rwanda, vetiver mulch raised maize to 8089 kg per hectare against 4755 on flat rainfed plots [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_1]. In Burkina Faso, crop yields in years of average rainfall rose by over 100 per cent on farms using zaï [ev_crop_yield_sawa11h1_1]. On crusted degraded soil in Burkina Faso, 30-cm zaï with compost gave 408 kg of millet per hectare where direct seeding gave none [ev_crop_yield_zour25h1_1]. In Zimbabwe's El Niño drought season, maize under no-till with a residue mulch yielded 31.8% more than under conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_mash25h1_1]. Primary trials and surveys from eastern and southern Africa now stand in for second-hand Zambia readings. In on-farm trials in Ethiopia, ripper plus tied ridging with fertiliser gave 1775 kg of maize per hectare against 1458 under conventional maresha ploughing with the same fertiliser, and 1076 against 945 kg of tef [ev_crop_yield_rock09_1, ev_crop_yield_rock09_4]; in Tanzania, ripping and pitting combined with fertilisation gave yields 1.5–2.2 times those of conventional ploughing with the same fertilisation [ev_crop_yield_rock09_11]; and at Chipata, Zambia, basins with fertiliser gave 6660 kg of maize per hectare against 3153 under conventional practice [ev_crop_yield_rock09_13]. In Zambia's 2001/2 season hand-hoe conservation-farming basins gave 3,054 kg of maize per hectare against 1,339 under ploughing, and a regression controlling for planting date, hybrid seed and fertiliser puts the gain from the basins themselves closer to 700 kg per hectare for maize and 400 to 500 kg for cotton [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_2, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_3]; a later survey of Zambian conservation-agriculture households reports 5.2 t of maize per hectare in basins against 1.8 under the hand hoe [ev_crop_yield_umar11_1]. A meta-analysis of tied-ridge-furrow experiments finds tied ridges without fertiliser or mulch yielded 17% more sorghum grain than flat planting [ev_crop_yield_makm21_1]. In Madagascar, rice sown without tillage on a dead mulch and rotated averaged 2.8 against 2.6 t per hectare on lowland and 2.4 against 2.1 on hillside fields, and year-to-year variability fell after consecutive years under the system (a 6% and a 13% decrease in the coefficient of variation) [ev_crop_yield_brue14_1, ev_crop_yield_brue14_2, ev_yield_stability_brue14_3, ev_yield_stability_brue14_4]. Crop-model (APSIM) runs on semi-arid Zimbabwe weather give higher maize yields under conservation agriculture than under ploughing when aggregated across seasons, and more stable yields across different types of seasons [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_5, ev_yield_stability_faocr11_6]. In a Zimbabwe household panel, conservation agriculture (mostly planting basins, with residue mulch and rotation on some plots) improved maize yields both when rainfall was above average and during times of drought, and sorghum and cowpea yields during drought [ev_crop_yield_mich19_3, ev_crop_yield_mich19_4, ev_crop_yield_mich19_5]. A review of conservation agriculture in Zambia also cites planting basins plus lime raising yields by 68% [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_1], a simulated gain of around 40% for the whole conservation farming package [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_6], higher soil moisture improving yields in poor seasons [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_3], and global syntheses: reduced tillage and crop residue management associated with a 106% increase in cereal yields, an average yield improvement of over 100% for smallholder conservation agriculture across 286 developing-country case studies, and a slight increase over conventional tillage, growing over time and especially in dry conditions, across 25 long-term trials [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_13, ev_crop_yield_arsl15_15, ev_crop_yield_arsl15_16]. Grain per unit of rain rises with capture in a set of East and Southern African trials: the best conservation-farming practice per site gave yield increases ranging from 20 to 120% over conventional tillage whilst rain water productivity improved with 10–50% [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. In an on-farm trial at Houndé, Burkina Faso, stone rows with zaï pits, every arm also receiving manure, raised maize grain to 4457 kg per hectare with NPK and urea against 2157 kg under the farmers' practice of oxen ploughing with NPK and urea, and to 3768 kg averaged over the fertility options, and lifted rain water productivity from 3.10 to 6.61 kg per hectare per mm [ev_crop_yield_koro17_1, ev_crop_yield_koro17_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_1]. A review reports that contour tied-ridging in eastern Sudan gave the highest water use efficiency of the treatments compared [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. The FAO compilers rate improving water productivity at the top of their scale for the conservation agriculture group [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_2].
justification.conditionality: Held out of the class, as a caveat on where the practice performs rather than as production evidence: in the Sudanian zone of Cameroon, where rain exceeds 80 mm a day and 1,200 mm a year, sorghum in zaï pits yielded less than flat-cultivated fields because of frequent waterlogging and the risk of nutrient leaching [ev_crop_yield_roose93_4]; 92% of the data in a conservation agriculture review show mulch cover in high-rainfall areas lowering yields through waterlogging [ev_crop_yield_rusin11_3]; and at sites with over 1,200 mm of seasonal rainfall conservation agriculture yielded 4.3% less than conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_corb20_7]. In a wetter sub-humid Kenyan site, ridged plots with fertiliser gave the lowest yields, slightly below conventional practice, which the authors say can probably be explained by waterlogging caused by ridging [ev_crop_yield_rock09_6]. Read these as a siting limit: in-situ capture should not be applied where rainfall is that heavy. In drought seasons gains vanish: conservation agriculture pillars had no detectable effect in a Kenyan season with a failed start, tied ridging gave no advantage in Kenyan short rains with meteorological droughts, and in Mozambique and Zimbabwe conservation agriculture gave no harvest or yielded less than conventional tillage [ev_crop_yield_boil19_3, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_2, ev_crop_yield_ndun23_5, ev_crop_yield_thierf15_1, ev_crop_yield_rusin11_7]. Much of the pit gain depends on manure or fertiliser (pits alone gave an average sorghum gain of only 38 kg/ha in one study against 310 kg/ha in another), the Zimbabwe planting-basin gain also carries manure and fertiliser, and the review ranges for pits are not pooled estimates [ev_crop_yield_mazv09_1, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_1]. In the Malawi El Nino survey banking, the reinforcement of ridges while the crop is growing, cut maize from 245 to 153 kg per hectare, so some in-field practices lowered yield in that season [ev_crop_yield_boil19_5]. Planting basins gave no significant gain over no mulch in 2011 at either Ethiopian site (4239 against 4171 and 4265 against 4131 kg per hectare) [ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_5, ev_crop_yield_sime15h2_7]. Rwandan contour ridges were not significantly different from flat rainfed plots (5937 against 4755 kg per hectare) [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_2]. The Burkina Faso zaï and half-moon contrasts are against land where direct seeding produced no grain, with compost added to the pits, so they measure bringing degraded land into production rather than an improvement on a cropped field. The Zimbabwe residue-mulch gain is one on-station season with no normal-year comparison, and the mulch is bundled with no-till [ev_crop_yield_mash25h1_1]. The East African and Zambian trial gains are bundles. In Ethiopia the comparator carried the same fertiliser, but without fertiliser neither improved tillage nor fertiliser alone raised maize significantly, and the 20–50% tef gain without fertiliser was not significant [ev_crop_yield_rock09_2, ev_crop_yield_rock09_3]; the Tanzanian ripping-or-pitting arms are bundled with reduced tillage [ev_crop_yield_rock09_11]; and the Chipata basins carried improved seed against a conventional practice with extremely low fertiliser, in seasons of well-above-average rainfall, a gain the authors say cannot be fully explained [ev_crop_yield_rock09_13]. Some trial arms lost: pitting with fertiliser was the lowest-yielding treatment at Machakos, at 1.2 against 1.6 t per hectare under conventional practice [ev_crop_yield_rock09_9], and at the more arid Kenyan sites each site recorded complete crop failures in two out of three and four seasons, which the treatments did not avert; water harvesting is not irrigation [ev_crop_yield_rock09_10]. The Zambian 2001/2 raw contrast is one season with no normal-year reference and mixes the basin effect with higher input use, since most basin farmers received hybrid seed, fertiliser and lime on credit; the regression figure is the cleaner estimate, and even its basin dummy also picks up extra weeding labour and lime [ev_crop_yield_hagg03_1, ev_crop_yield_hagg03_2]. The later Zambian survey yields are farmer self-reports with large spreads, and the basin gain over ploughing (5.2 against 3.8 t per hectare) was not significant [ev_crop_yield_umar11_1, ev_crop_yield_umar11_2]; a national Zambian smallholder panel finds no significant maize yield effect of planting basins under any of its estimators [ev_crop_yield_burk12_1]; and paired soil samples on Zambian fields under basins or ripping (bundled with reduced tillage), with residues hardly retained, showed no significant difference in nitrogen [ev_soil_nitrogen_umar11_6]. The Zimbabwe panel keeps drought-season and normal-season results apart: in average rainfall periods conservation agriculture had no significant impact on any crop, in another specification it decreased maize yields by itself, and it did not mitigate rainfall-shortfall or surplus losses for millet and groundnut, so its gains appear only in seasons away from the average [ev_crop_yield_mich19_1, ev_crop_yield_mich19_2, ev_crop_yield_mich19_6, ev_crop_yield_mich19_7]. The tied-ridge meta-analysis finds no significant millet gain over flat planting and no significant difference when grass mulch was added to the ridges, and its sorghum observation count is internally inconsistent [ev_crop_yield_makm21_3, ev_crop_yield_makm21_2, ev_crop_yield_makm21_1]. In Madagascar the severe drought of 2007–2008 could not be offset by the system, and the pooled comparison showed no change in yield variance, the stability gain appearing only after consecutive years; the rice gains bundle no-till, mulch and rotation [ev_crop_yield_brue14_5, ev_yield_stability_brue14_7]. The crop-model results are simulations that bundle residue cover, better infiltration and fertiliser targeting; under sub-humid weather the model gives no difference [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_4], and in seasons with 230 mm and 176 mm of in-crop rainfall there was total crop failure under both systems [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_2]. Farmer reports of basin yields of >1 tonnes per hectare in poor-rainfall seasons, against total failure under ploughing, compare fertilised basins with unfertilised ploughing, which the author calls too confounded [ev_crop_yield_faocr11_9]. The remaining Zambia and global figures are cited secondhand in Arslan and colleagues' literature review, and none has a normal-year comparison: the 68% gain is for planting basins plus lime application, with timely conventional farming giving 50% in the same trials [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_1]; the roughly 40% gain is a simulation of the whole conservation farming package, through early planting and improved soil quality [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_6]; the 106% is for reduced tillage together with residue management [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_13]; the poor-season result bundles reduced tillage with residue retention [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_3]; the over-100% figure comes from purposely selected best-practice projects [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_15]; and the long-term trials are mainly from North America, Australia and Europe [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_16]. Readings in that review that misread their primaries were dropped, and the primaries themselves are now in the pool directly. Those best-practice arms are bundled: planting pits, basins or ripper-with-ridging (the capture element, which is the practice here) come with reduced tillage and mostly with fertiliser, and tillage alone is not water harvesting [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_1]. The trial-level readings are weaker: the authors find no clear tillage effect on rain water productivity in Kenya, no clear effects of tillage in Ethiopia (where the gains that do show come with fertilised treatments), and only a tendency of improvement in semi-arid Tanzania [ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_rock09_4]. The Burkina Faso trial covers the 2014 season only, and every conservation arm also received manure, so its gains belong to the package rather than to the structures alone [ev_crop_yield_koro17_1, ev_crop_yield_koro17_7]. At Houndé, grass strips with zaï (3507 kg per hectare with NPK and urea, 3065 kg averaged, against 2157 kg) were not significantly different from the control in yield, nor in rain water productivity (4.84 against 3.10) [ev_crop_yield_koro17_2, ev_crop_yield_koro17_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_2]. At Péni no conservation arm differed significantly from the control in yield or water productivity, grass strips with zaï giving 4192 kg and earth bunds with contour ploughing 4067 kg against 3317 kg per hectare; the authors attribute this to rainfall, saying water was not a limiting factor at Péni [ev_crop_yield_koro17_5, ev_crop_yield_koro17_6, ev_crop_yield_koro17_7, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_koro17_4]. The Sudan comparison ranks treatments without a no-practice value [ev_rain_water_productivity_ngur26_3]. That rating is a compiler judgement for a group that bundles mulch with minimum tillage and rotation, so it does not isolate the soil-cover capture element [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_2].

effect_mechanism: Semi-circular bunds, Vallerani micro-catchments and trenches harvest runoff for crops and grasses: WOCAT compilers report crop production and biomass augmented several times over traditional techniques with the Vallerani System in Burkina Faso, higher millet and straw yields from cropland bunds on abandoned farmland in Niger, and more fodder and grazing days. Negarim micro-catchments with supplementary irrigation supported fruit production at Embrapa Semi-Arid in Brazil, and semi-circular bunds raised millet grain production under African conditions. A review tabulates crop yield increases of 50–200% from half-moons in Burkina Faso and Niger, and cites micro-basin water harvesting in Zambia doubling maize yields to 3 t per hectare [ev_crop_yield_ngur26_2, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_5]. On crusted degraded soil in Burkina Faso, 1-m half-moons with compost gave 1372 kg of millet per hectare where direct seeding gave none [ev_crop_yield_zour25h1_2]. The WOCAT guideline authors rate improving water productivity for the microcatchment group at the lowest positive mark on their scale, below their marks for crop production and reduced risk of production failure [ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_4].
conditionality: Apart from an FAO manual citing earlier work and a review quoting ranges from earlier studies, all units are practitioner judgements from technology sheets, not measurements. Animal production was rated lower for trenches and semi-circular bunds in Niger because treated rangeland must be protected from grazing for the first years while vegetation establishes. The review figures are ranges and single citations rather than pooled estimates [ev_crop_yield_ngur26_2, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_5]. The Burkina Faso zaï and half-moon contrasts are against land where direct seeding produced no grain, with compost added to the pits, so they measure bringing degraded land into production rather than an improvement on a cropped field. It is the one measured unit in this row [ev_crop_yield_zour25h1_2]. That is a group-level judgement by the guideline authors, direction only [ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_4].

effect_mechanism: Sand dams, small reservoirs, subsurface dams, farm ponds, check dams and haffirs store runoff that farmers use to irrigate more land and take a second or dry-season crop, while sediment trapped behind check dams can be planted with fodder; in Kenya sand-dam water lets farmers irrigate more crops and raise production, and in Brazil soil management in subsurface dams raised crop productivity [ev_crop_yield_ritc21_1, ev_crop_yield_brito07_5, ev_crop_yield_wocat_1474_2011_crop_production, ev_crop_yield_wocat_2844_2017_crop_production, ev_forage_productivity_wocat_6716_2023_fodder_production]. WOCAT compilers in Somalia describe reliable irrigation from a haffir improving tomato and watermelon, grasses regenerating around the dam, and better water and fodder raising animal production [ev_crop_yield_wocat_7777_2026_crop_production, ev_forage_productivity_wocat_7777_2026_fodder_production, ev_livestock_productivity_wocat_7777_2026_animal_production]. Sand dams in Kenya cut crop failure against a control catchment, and in Zimbabwe improved water availability improved livestock health where cattle had been driven up to 20 km to water [ev_crop_yield_lasage08_1, ev_livestock_productivity_lazurko24_1]. Stored water also stabilises output: Indian farmers reported crop-failure chances falling from 20% to 6% in the rainy season and from 100% to 5–10% in winter with a farm pond, reviews report rainwater harvesting systems stabilising production under intra-seasonal rainfall variability and supplemental irrigation of 50–200 mm bridging critical dry spells, wheat output in Pakistan rose from 450 to 815 kg over seven years after small reservoirs were built, a bundle of moisture conservation, rainwater harvesting and micro-irrigation in India raised system productivity by 25%, and silt farmland behind check dams on China's Loess Plateau yields 6–10 times more than sloping farmland [ev_yield_stability_pals23_1, ev_yield_stability_pals23_2, ev_yield_stability_silv26_1, ev_yield_stability_rock10_1, ev_crop_yield_silv26_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_silv26_1, ev_crop_yield_luca21_1]. In Rwanda, runoff from the terrace waterways collected in a dug, lined pond and applied to maize by a gravity drip kit as supplementary irrigation gave 11982 kg per hectare against 4755 on flat rainfed plots [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_3]. The WOCAT guideline authors rate improving water productivity for the macrocatchment group at the middle mark of their scale [ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_3].
conditionality: Most units are practitioner ratings from WOCAT technology sheets, and the literature units are largely reviews citing earlier studies, an expert's personal communication on livestock, and Brazilian case accounts from an upper-middle-income setting [ev_crop_yield_ritc21_1, ev_livestock_productivity_veno12_1, ev_crop_yield_cirilo03_4]. A Brazilian subsurface dam produced no harvest in a year of adverse weather, and an Indian farm-pond sheet rates fodder production unchanged; fodder and livestock outcomes enter only as components of the production gap [ev_crop_yield_brito07_6, ev_forage_productivity_wocat_1474_2011_fodder_production]. The Kenyan and Zimbabwean sand-dam findings come from interviews and respondent statements [ev_crop_yield_lasage08_1, ev_livestock_productivity_lazurko24_1]. Soil salinisation may appear on check-dam farmland, the Pakistani wheat figure has no area denominator, the Indian productivity gain bundles micro-irrigation, and the pond figures come from a farmer survey reported in a preprint [ev_crop_yield_luca21_1, ev_crop_yield_silv26_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_silv26_1, ev_yield_stability_pals23_2]. The Rwandan pond result is a bundle — terrace runoff capture, a lined storage pond and drip irrigation — so the yield is delivered through irrigation hardware and cannot be read as a pure capture effect; it is one season of a randomised trial in which every plot received farmyard manure and mineral fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_3]. That is a group-level judgement by the guideline authors, direction only [ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_3].

justification.mechanism: Sand dams, small reservoirs, subsurface dams, farm ponds, check dams and haffirs store runoff that farmers use to irrigate more land and take a second or dry-season crop, while sediment trapped behind check dams can be planted with fodder; in Kenya sand-dam water lets farmers irrigate more crops and raise production, and in Brazil soil management in subsurface dams raised crop productivity [ev_crop_yield_ritc21_1, ev_crop_yield_brito07_5, ev_crop_yield_wocat_1474_2011_crop_production, ev_crop_yield_wocat_2844_2017_crop_production, ev_forage_productivity_wocat_6716_2023_fodder_production]. WOCAT compilers in Somalia describe reliable irrigation from a haffir improving tomato and watermelon, grasses regenerating around the dam, and better water and fodder raising animal production [ev_crop_yield_wocat_7777_2026_crop_production, ev_forage_productivity_wocat_7777_2026_fodder_production, ev_livestock_productivity_wocat_7777_2026_animal_production]. Sand dams in Kenya cut crop failure against a control catchment, and in Zimbabwe improved water availability improved livestock health where cattle had been driven up to 20 km to water [ev_crop_yield_lasage08_1, ev_livestock_productivity_lazurko24_1]. Stored water also stabilises output: Indian farmers reported crop-failure chances falling from 20% to 6% in the rainy season and from 100% to 5–10% in winter with a farm pond, reviews report rainwater harvesting systems stabilising production under intra-seasonal rainfall variability and supplemental irrigation of 50–200 mm bridging critical dry spells, wheat output in Pakistan rose from 450 to 815 kg over seven years after small reservoirs were built, a bundle of moisture conservation, rainwater harvesting and micro-irrigation in India raised system productivity by 25%, and silt farmland behind check dams on China's Loess Plateau yields 6–10 times more than sloping farmland [ev_yield_stability_pals23_1, ev_yield_stability_pals23_2, ev_yield_stability_silv26_1, ev_yield_stability_rock10_1, ev_crop_yield_silv26_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_silv26_1, ev_crop_yield_luca21_1]. In Rwanda, runoff from the terrace waterways collected in a dug, lined pond and applied to maize by a gravity drip kit as supplementary irrigation gave 11982 kg per hectare against 4755 on flat rainfed plots [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_3]. The WOCAT guideline authors rate improving water productivity for the macrocatchment group at the middle mark of their scale [ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_3].
justification.conditionality: Most units are practitioner ratings from WOCAT technology sheets, and the literature units are largely reviews citing earlier studies, an expert's personal communication on livestock, and Brazilian case accounts from an upper-middle-income setting [ev_crop_yield_ritc21_1, ev_livestock_productivity_veno12_1, ev_crop_yield_cirilo03_4]. A Brazilian subsurface dam produced no harvest in a year of adverse weather, and an Indian farm-pond sheet rates fodder production unchanged; fodder and livestock outcomes enter only as components of the production gap [ev_crop_yield_brito07_6, ev_forage_productivity_wocat_1474_2011_fodder_production]. The Kenyan and Zimbabwean sand-dam findings come from interviews and respondent statements [ev_crop_yield_lasage08_1, ev_livestock_productivity_lazurko24_1]. Soil salinisation may appear on check-dam farmland, the Pakistani wheat figure has no area denominator, the Indian productivity gain bundles micro-irrigation, and the pond figures come from a farmer survey reported in a preprint [ev_crop_yield_luca21_1, ev_crop_yield_silv26_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_silv26_1, ev_yield_stability_pals23_2]. The Rwandan pond result is a bundle — terrace runoff capture, a lined storage pond and drip irrigation — so the yield is delivered through irrigation hardware and cannot be read as a pure capture effect; it is one season of a randomised trial in which every plot received farmyard manure and mineral fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_uwiz18h1_3]. That is a group-level judgement by the guideline authors, direction only [ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_3].

effect_mechanism: Jessour in Tunisia, water spreading in Sudan, spate irrigation in Eritrea, marab floodplain farming in Jordan and water-spreading weirs in Ethiopia divert and spread floodwater over fields as spate or supplementary irrigation, and compilers rate crop and fodder production as increased [ev_crop_yield_wocat_6715_2023_crop_production, ev_crop_yield_wocat_1013_2011_crop_production, ev_crop_yield_wocat_1333_2010_crop_production]. Much of the gain is fed to livestock: crops in the Jordan marab are used as fodder, crop residues in Eritrea feed animals, and Ethiopian compilers link fodder gains to the soil and moisture conserved behind the structure [ev_crop_yield_wocat_5770_2020_crop_production, ev_forage_productivity_wocat_1333_2010_fodder_production, ev_forage_productivity_wocat_6715_2023_fodder_production]. The WOCAT guideline authors rate improving water productivity for the floodwater harvesting group at the lowest positive mark on their scale [ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_2].
conditionality: Every unit is a practitioner rating from a WOCAT technology sheet; there is no literature measurement in this cell. The Ethiopian rating is stated as the expert's conviction, and the Sudan rating is relative to nothing being grown otherwise, so the scale of the gain is a counterfactual judgement rather than a yield comparison [ev_crop_yield_wocat_6715_2023_crop_production, ev_crop_yield_wocat_1292_2015_crop_production]. That is a group-level judgement by the guideline authors, direction only [ev_rain_water_productivity_wocwh13_2].

effect_mechanism: Terraces, fanya juu and contour stone bunds or lines level slopes and slow runoff so more water and soil stay on the field; yields of maize, barley, millet and sorghum rose on terraced or bunded land, especially in dry years. Stone bunds raised sorghum yields by 33% to 55% in Burkina Faso and by about 142% with compost, and millet yields in Niger rose by more than 40% up to 15 years after the bunds were built [ev_crop_yield_zoug14_2, ev_crop_yield_zoug14_4, ev_crop_yield_zoug14_1_s]. WOCAT compilers add that stone lines in Tunisia protect farmland from degradation, contour stone bunds in Bhutan enlarge the cultivable area as stones are removed, and Gradoni orchard terraces in Uzbekistan turn unproductive land productive [ev_crop_yield_wocat_6610_2022_crop_production, ev_crop_yield_wocat_6891_2023_crop_production, ev_crop_yield_wocat_7553_2025_crop_production]. Meta-analyses support the gain: a meta-analysis of traditional in-situ water harvesting finds a 48% yield increase for terraces, an Ethiopian synthesis a mean gain of 322 kg per hectare for stone bunds with soil total nitrogen up from 0.16 to 0.20%, and a terracing meta-analysis finds biomass on terraces about 1.94 times that on slopes, and reviewed studies report terraced teff, barley and maize yields at least two times those on slopes and 20% gains on young bench terraces in Peru [ev_crop_yield_wei16_1, ev_crop_yield_wei16_2, ev_crop_yield_wei16_4]; reviewed studies also report maize yields up nearly 50% on fanya juu terraces in semi-arid Kenya, wheat yields 6–7 times higher on stone-wall terraces than on slopes under the same input costs, and land productivity over 19% higher on bench terraces [ev_crop_yield_tefe24_5, ev_crop_yield_adim16_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_adim16_1, ev_crop_yield_ngur26_4, ev_crop_yield_wei16_3, ev_agricultural_production_value_wei16_1]. In Burkina Faso, crop yields in years of average rainfall rose by 63–74 per cent on farms using rock bunds [ev_crop_yield_sawa11h1_2]. The FAO compilers rate improving water productivity for the cross-slope barrier group at the middle mark of their scale [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_3].
conditionality: Several literature figures are lender self-reports (Rwanda before/after yields, Indian with/without models bundled with crop packages); the Rwanda value-of-harvest gain is from an independent DIME evaluation, and the Burkina Faso and Niger gains are cited from earlier studies, the largest bundled with compost [ev_crop_yield_rwa18_7, ev_crop_yield_utk22_8, ev_agricultural_production_value_rwa18_3, ev_crop_yield_zoug14_4]. Diversion banquettes in Niger reduced yields, progressive terraces on poor soils in Rwanda gave no yield increase, bench terraces need heavy fertility restoration before yields rise, and a Haitian compiler notes that on very degraded land farmers must wait for the soil to recover [ev_crop_yield_heusch95_1, ev_crop_yield_roose06_3, ev_crop_yield_roose94_4, ev_crop_yield_wocat_3223_2017_crop_production]. Most pooled units are practitioner ratings from WOCAT sheets rather than measurements. Stone bunds in semi-arid Tanzania reduced maize yield by 13% [ev_crop_yield_adim16_9], and in Algeria farmers lost 5 to 15% of their cropped area to banquettes without seeing yields improve, legume yields between banquettes showed no significant gain, and a Moroccan farmer saw no yield improvement between banquettes imposed by technicians [ev_crop_yield_arab04_1, ev_crop_yield_arab04_2, ev_crop_yield_roos10_2]. The terracing meta-analysis pools unweighted ratios and several of the largest multiples are single studies cited in reviews [ev_crop_yield_wei16_1, ev_crop_yield_wei16_3]. The Burkina Faso rock-bund gain is for years the authors call average rainfall, with compost on the bunded fields [ev_crop_yield_sawa11h1_2]. That is a compiler judgement for a group spanning earth bunds, stone lines, vegetative strips and fanya juu terraces, direction only [ev_rain_water_productivity_faoslm11_3].

effect_mechanism: Higher and more stable yields, irrigation of gardens and higher-value crops from stored water, and better fodder and livestock raise household income and food security; beneficiaries shift from staples to vegetables, and a quasi-experimental study cited in a review found soil and water conservation raised net rice profit in Ghana by a significant 16 per cent [ev_household_income_veno12_2, ev_food_security_cirilo03_6, ev_economic_return_mala24_1]. WOCAT compilers describe the same pathway: planting pits in Uganda keep banana stands fruiting through drought and raise harvests for sale, ripper tillage in Zambia gives better tolerance to dry spells at lower tillage cost, farm ponds in Cambodia supply irrigation during drought, and contour stone bunds in Bhutan enlarge the cultivable area for diverse crops [ev_food_security_wocat_1587_2013_risk_of_production_failure, ev_household_income_wocat_1587_2013_farm_income, ev_food_security_wocat_1139_2013_risk_of_production_failure, ev_household_income_wocat_1139_2013_farm_income, ev_food_security_wocat_2844_2017_risk_of_production_failure, ev_food_security_wocat_6891_2023_risk_of_production_failure]. WOCAT compilers' own benefit-versus-cost ratings point the same way, judging the long-term returns on both establishment and maintenance positive or very positive on nearly every sheet. In Kenya, farmers living near sand dams saw average income rise by 60% as more water in dry periods raised farm yields [ev_household_income_lasage08_1]. An Ethiopian synthesis reports positive net present values of 3486.2 Birr per hectare for stone bunds, 2794.0 for bench terraces and 5283.4 for level fanya juu [ev_economic_return_adim16_1, ev_economic_return_adim16_2, ev_economic_return_adim16_3]; In Zimbabwe first-year planting-basin farmers earned a maize gross margin of 473.36 USD per hectare against 70.60 on conventional plots in the low-rainfall budget, with 866.84 against 357.16 for experienced farmers in high rainfall [ev_economic_return_mazv09_1, ev_economic_return_mazv09_2]; and ground cover raised the odds of a Malawian plot meeting the household maize requirement in the El Niño season, and planting basins sharply raised those odds in a good Kenyan season [ev_food_security_boil19_1, ev_food_security_boil19_2]. Reviews add that rainwater-harvesting ponds brought statistically significant gains in household income and food security in Burkina Faso, water storage gave Ethiopian smallholders greater income security, harvested water used with precision irrigation in Ethiopia reached a net water value of up to 1.53 USD per cubic metre, and benefit-cost ratios of up to 3.38 with payback periods of 6.8 to 12 years; Indian farms with a farm pond reported net returns of 857 USD per hectare against 586 without [ev_household_income_silv26_1, ev_household_income_silv26_2, ev_economic_return_silv26_1, ev_economic_return_silv26_2, ev_economic_return_pals23_1]. Modelled bench-terrace gains in Peru could raise per capita incomes by up to 15%, and a review tabulates significantly increased food security and incomes from check dams and infiltration pits in Malawi [ev_household_income_wei16_1, ev_food_security_ngur26_1]. Against the fertilised conventional arm in the same Zimbabwe budget the first-year margin was 473.36 against 48.19 US dollars per hectare [ev_economic_return_mazv09_3]. In Zimbabwe's El Niño season, no-till with a residue mulch returned a cost-benefit ratio of 1.39 against 1.05 for conventional tillage [ev_economic_return_mash25h1_3]. A review cites reduced tillage with residue maintained giving the highest net benefit and marginal rate of return on teff [ev_economic_return_tade23h1_4]. On crusted degraded soil in Burkina Faso, 1-m half-moons with compost were profitable at 377 275 FCFA per hectare after the investment [ev_economic_return_zour25h1_3]. Higher yields are cited as improving household food security in Burkina Faso, especially on farms that apply manure or some kind of soil and water conservation on over half their plots [ev_food_security_sawa11h1_5]. A review cites soil and water conservation measures, including level bunds and fanya juu terraces, boosting farmer income by increasing soil fertility, yield and water [ev_household_income_tade23h1_1]. In Zambia, crop budgets for hand-hoe conservation-farming basins give returns per hectare 70 percent higher than conventional hand hoe cultivation and 150 percent higher than conventional plowing for cotton, and returns to land and to peak-season labor 60 to 90 percent higher than hand hoe tillage for maize [ev_economic_return_hagg03_6, ev_economic_return_hagg03_7, ev_economic_return_hagg03_8]. In Brazil, an Embrapa survey of some communities found small-farm incomes rose by about half a minimum wage per month after the second filling of the barraginhas, and adopters rated food security as the technology's largest impact [ev_household_income_mira19_1, ev_food_security_mira19_2].
conditionality: The roll-up states conflicting evidence because the sub-practice rows disagree: the runoff-catchment, micro-catchment, spate and terracing rows each lean positive, while the in-field and cross-family rows are each split between gains and losses. What pulls the in-field side apart is how the gain is valued and against what. Crop budgets built on bundled input packages, and the practitioner ratings, put basins well ahead [ev_economic_return_hagg03_6, ev_economic_return_hagg03_8, ev_economic_return_mazv09_1]; but a Zimbabwe household panel that values predicted yields with inputs held constant finds conservation agriculture (mostly planting basins, with residue mulch and rotation on some plots) generates less revenue than traditional cultivation over a large portion of the rainfall distribution, and its revenue comes out ahead only when rainfall is far from the mean [ev_economic_return_mich19_8]. The other losses are season- or practice-specific: banking in Malawi's El Nino season, tied ridging in a Kenyan drought season, and 30-cm zaï on a Burkina Faso trial [ev_food_security_boil19_3, ev_economic_return_ndun23_1, ev_economic_return_zour25h1_4]. In the cross-family row, gains from bundled programmes and cistern income sit against costs exceeding gains: single soil and water conservation measures not covering their annual costs in Burkina Faso, negative net present values for graded Ethiopian structures, a Brazilian production-cistern benefit-cost ratio far below break-even, and Niger families with soil and water conservation still in deficit in low-rainfall years [ev_economic_return_zoug14_3, ev_economic_return_adim16_4, ev_economic_return_casag22_9, ev_food_security_kabo04_1]; there farm size, how household labour is costed, where structures are built and the rainfall year separate the sides. Most pooled units are practitioner ratings from WOCAT technology sheets, including compilers' benefit-versus-cost judgements rather than measured returns, and much of the literature comes from bundled watershed programmes and lender completion or appraisal reports, so measured household effects are a minority. Independent evaluations are more cautious: no significant effect on food security or total income in Ethiopian programmes, terraces reducing net crop income, a Brazilian production-cistern programme with a benefit-cost ratio far below break-even, single SWC measures not covering their annual costs, and sand dams likely not cost-efficient [ev_food_security_abate21_4, ev_food_security_arega24_1, ev_household_income_mala24_1, ev_economic_return_casag22_9, ev_economic_return_zoug14_3, ev_economic_return_ritc21_1]. Compilers also rate check-dam land in China as raising the risk of production failure in extreme wet years and record no change on several sheets, including a subsistence farm pond in India; Kenyan sand dams sit inside a wider food-security programme, and food security, income and returns are all proxies for poverty [ev_food_security_wocat_1455_2011_risk_of_production_failure, ev_household_income_wocat_1474_2011_farm_income, ev_food_security_wocat_1537_2012_food_security_selfsufficiency]. Short-term returns on establishment are rated slightly to very negative on sheets from Tunisia, China, Rwanda, Yemen, Cabo Verde, Nicaragua, Jordan, Uzbekistan and Somalia, reflecting up-front costs that are only recovered over time. The Kenyan sand-dam income rise compares a small sample of households with a control catchment [ev_household_income_lasage08_1]. New evidence adds further limits: the same synthesis reports negative net present values for graded fanya juu (−148 Birr per hectare) and graded soil bunds (−708 Birr per hectare), possibly because off-site benefits were left out [ev_economic_return_adim16_4]; cost savings from conservation agriculture are usually small for smallholders; and in a Kenyan drought season net benefits were higher without tied ridging [ev_economic_return_corb20_1, ev_economic_return_ndun23_1]. The Zimbabwe planting-basin margins include manure and fertiliser and the high-rainfall figure is a sensitivity scenario, the Indian pond returns are cross-sectional from a preprint survey confounded by farm size and assets, the reviewed income and water-value figures are secondary citations at their upper end, and the Peruvian income gain is modelled [ev_economic_return_mazv09_2, ev_economic_return_pals23_1, ev_economic_return_silv26_2, ev_household_income_wei16_1]. In Malawi's El Nino season banking lowered the odds of a plot meeting the household maize requirement from 0.19 to 0.054, so a mis-timed in-field practice can cut food security rather than raise it [ev_food_security_boil19_3]. 30-cm zaï on the same Burkina Faso trial ran at a loss (−98 624 FCFA per hectare), smaller than the direct-seeding loss, and the investment counted is the experiment's own cost [ev_economic_return_zour25h1_4]. The Zimbabwe ratio is a single drought-season budget with the mulch bundled with no-till [ev_economic_return_mash25h1_3]. The teff returns are cited second-hand [ev_economic_return_tade23h1_4]. The Burkina Faso food-security statement is cited and does not separate manure from soil and water conservation [ev_food_security_sawa11h1_5]. The Ethiopian income claim is cited from a study that the citing review itself describes as methodologically weak [ev_household_income_tade23h1_1]. The Zambian returns are crop budgets with output estimated from regression coefficients, bundled with early planting and purchased inputs (hybrid seed and fertiliser for maize), and the authors say early-planting gains dominate the maize results [ev_economic_return_hagg03_6, ev_economic_return_hagg03_8]. The Zimbabwe panel figure is gross revenue at later market prices with labour and non-market inputs unvalued, so it is neither a profit nor a poverty measure [ev_economic_return_mich19_8]. The barraginha income and food-security findings are Embrapa's self-assessment of its own technology, from an informal survey and adopter ratings with no normal-year reference [ev_household_income_mira19_1, ev_food_security_mira19_2].
